An Indic Voice Agent with CUGA

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (755 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English.
  • According to recent reports, we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness.
  • It has been revealed that A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most useful knowledge is written and digitized in English. Most of the people who need it speak, and think, in their own regional languages like Hindi, Tamil, Telugu, Gujarati, Marathi and many others. Many would rather talk than type.

According to recent reports, we built a small voice agent to close that gap, using CUGA as the agent harness. This post explains the use case and what we learned. You can try it yourself in CUGA Apps.

It has been revealed that A farmer asks a question aloud, in their own language: how do I tell good seed from bad? The agent:.

If someone asks about cricket or coding, it politely steers them back to farming instead of making something up.

Sources indicate that CUGA (ConfigUrable Generalist Agent) is IBM Research's open-source agent harness. It handles the model wiring, tool management, state and guardrails, so you write tools and a prompt instead of the agent loop. Here we use it as an embedded SDK inside a small web app, for three things:.

The key design idea is simple: CUGA is a text-in, text-out brain. Voice is two thin layers around it.

Because the agent only ever sees text, you can build and test it with plain text first, then add the ears and the mouth. You can also swap speech providers without touching the agent. We support two: Sarvam AI's cloud speech APIs, called directly from the user's browser, and open-source models (SraVaani for speech-to-text, Svara for text-to-speech) running on your own server.

Adding speech is the easy part. The hard part is cross-lingual retrieval: a Hindi question has to find an English paragraph.

Search works by turning text into vectors and finding the nearest ones. CUGA's default embedding model is English-only, so it turns Hindi into vectors that carry almost no meaning. With it, a Hindi or Tamil question still retrieves five passages, but they are the wrong ones. The model, correctly told to answer only from what it was given, quietly indicates "the handbook doesn't cover that". Every layer behaves correctly, so there is no error and no warning.

The fix is to use a multilingual embedding model (we use intfloat/multilingual-e5-large), so the same meaning lands in the same place whatever the language. Conceptually simple, though wiring it into CUGA took a small workaround (shown in the tutorial). After that, one English document serves every language, and you do not need translated copies of anything.

Our advice: before you tune a single prompt, ask your agent one question in a non-English language and check that it finds the right pages.

A few small decisions mattered more than we expected:.

Sources indicate that you do not need to set anything up to see it work. Open the voice agent in CUGA Apps on Hugging Face Spaces, ask a farming question in your language, and listen to the answer:.

Want to build one yourself? Our step-by-step tutorial, Build an Indic Voice Agent with CUGA, starts from an empty folder and adds each layer in turn.

In a recent development, nothing here is specific to agriculture. Swap the handbook for scheme documents, health advisories, or legal guides, and you have a different assistant. Swap the speech provider and you change the deployment model, such as cloud for speed or on-premises for data sovereignty, without rewriting the agent.

Recent findings suggest that voice-first, multilingual assistants are how digital services can reach people who were never served well by English-only text screens. Building them on an open, auditable harness, with answers tied to sources people can check, is how they earn trust.

According to recent reports, this approach sits precisely at the intersection of what we are building with IBM Bharat Core. Bharat Core is an optimized AI stack built on top of IBM Sovereign Core, designed specifically for the Indian ecosystem to run Indic AI workloads securely on local infrastructure. When scaling a voice agent from a prototype to a secure enterprise application (like a vernacular KYC system or multilingual government bot), you need greater control over data sovereignty. By pairing CUGA’s flexible agent harness with Bharat Core’s ready-to-deploy Indic connectors and fine-tuned models, developers can build fully compliant, sovereign AI solutions tailored to India's unique linguistic diversity.

If you are building for India at scale, see the work happening at IBM Bharat Core.

What should “Show me one” actually show?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (438 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Dev

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • “Show me one” is live on PasteCharm now.
  • The two buttons came out of a comment thread about one line of copy.
  • I had two ways to introduce the Bio Builder: “Pick a template” and “Stuck on what to put in your bio?”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Show me one” is live on PasteCharm now. It jumps to a finished bio you can read on the same page. You can look at it without changing anything you've already typed. There's a separate button to load it into the editor.

The two buttons came out of a comment thread about one line of copy.

I had two ways to introduce the Bio Builder: “Pick a template” and “Stuck on what to put in your bio?”.

Sources indicate that abdullah preferred the first. The action was clear from the first few words, and he expected to reach a template he could edit. Chu preferred the question for someone who was already stuck. He suggested “Show me one” as the button because it answers the question the page just asked.

In a recent development, before the update, you could start editing as soon as you reached the page. If you wanted to see a full template, there was a shortcut to the gallery. The fresh version puts one complete example next to the headline. You can see the name, the description, and the project line together before deciding to use it.

On the updated Bio Builder, Show me one takes you to the Indie Builder example. Use this template loads those words into the editor so you can make them yours. If you want more options, Browse all templates takes you to the gallery.

It has been revealed that that distinction matters when there's already something in the editor. Taking a look leaves your draft alone. Loading a template replaces it, and Undo template brings your previous draft back.

It has been revealed that chu pointed out something I'd missed. Someone who has never seen PasteCharm can tell me which headline sounds better. Someone who actually needs to write or update a bio this week can tell me what they'd expect the tool to give them.

Recent findings suggest that I'd show each person one headline, with the button and example out of view. Then I'd ask, “If you clicked through from here, what would you expect to see?” I'd write down their answer, reveal the page, and watch where they go to start their own bio. The question version is live. I don't have a comparison result yet.

If you're updating a profile this week, here's the question I'd actually ask you: When you read “Show me one,” did you expect to see a finished example, a list of templates, or a bio already loaded into an editor?

This article was drafted with AI from PasteCharm’s shipped changes and the public DEV discussion.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

In a recent development, the FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Industry observers note that not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently reveals that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

The golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

It has been revealed that the biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

Recent findings suggest that for couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you strategy intentionally from the start.

#127275. Latest Update: A Clock Made of Branches

📅 01 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (988 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fzakaria ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: A Clock Made of Branches

📅 01 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fzakaria

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, what is time inside a machine you want to replay?
  • Industry observers note that when building Rewind, a deterministic VM, you come face-to-face with the idea of how to represent time very rapidly.
  • You can’t simply record the wall-clock time of the host because time spent between two interception points depends on things outside the guest, like host load, CPU frequency, caches and other processes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, what is time inside a machine you want to replay? 🧘.

Industry observers note that when building Rewind, a deterministic VM, you come face-to-face with the idea of how to represent time very rapidly. You need a way to measure time inside the guest so that on subsequent replays, the guest sees the same time and makes the same decisions. Time is the ultimate variable.

You can’t simply record the wall-clock time of the host because time spent between two interception points depends on things outside the guest, like host load, CPU frequency, caches and other processes. Therefore the same guest work can take a different amount of time on the host.

Sources indicate that in dafuq is a deterministic VM? I explained how the clock inside Rewind VM moves 5 microseconds per step. More specifically, that clock, exit time, moves only when the guest exits such as from a syscall. It treats everything the program does between two exits as instant. Therefore a program that is CPU bound such as doing nothing but math for a full second between two system calls, sees only 5µs go by. 🤦🏻‍♂️.

Industry observers note that rewind has a second clock mode as well, counter time, that tries to account for the work. The clock advances one nanosecond for every conditional branch the guest retired.11This is the same approach popularized by the rr debugger. The rr paper calls it deterministic time.

Aside: New to Rewind? Start with a flaky build you only catch once and dafuq is a deterministic VM?

Still confused about what I mean by “free” and “branches”? Let’s look at a simple example to distinguish between the two clocks.

The counter time tries to account for the work whereas the exit time only advanced the clock on exits.22The 5µs was my guess at a reasonable cost of a system call and context switch on current hardware. The 1ns is roughly what a conditional branch costs on a current core.

We already understand that we cannot rely on the wall-clock time of the host. We need something to measure that is the same for every run of the same program so that we can equate it to time spent.

In a recent development, the guest’s instruction stream! The CPU is a deterministic machine: the same input, the same registers, the same memory, and the same instructions produce the same next state.

Sources indicate that we can measure time by measuring progress through the instruction stream. 💡.

Recent findings suggest that turns out that CPU manufacturers even ship a hardware counter for exactly that. Is it reliable? Let’s see. 🧐.

Let’s use this simple program: count down from a billion.

The assembly equivalent contains a mov, a billion dec+jnz (conditional branch) pairs, then three instructions to exit for a total of 2,000,000,004 instructions.

Let’s run it on the CPU twice and count the instructions and conditional branches with perf stat:.

Sources indicate that the same program and input gives the same conditional branch count, but the instruction count is off by a thousand or so. Why?

According to recent reports, although this loop is CPU bound and only decrements a register, it is still not isolated from the effects of the outside world. Timers tick, network packets arrive, other cores send inter-processor interrupts (IPIs). The program can’t see any of that, but the instruction counter we are probing can.

I pinned the loop to a single CPU and counted how many interrupts that CPU took during each run, from /proc/interrupts.

The dashed line is one extra count per interrupt, and the instruction counter is almost perfectly on it.33The fit is 0.94 rather than 1 because /proc/interrupts also catches the interrupts that land while perf and taskset start up and tear down, before and after the loop runs. The conditional branch counter on the other hand, stays at zero no matter how many interrupts land.

Sources indicate that interrupts from the outside-world are not the only thing that can skew the instruction count. The program can also page fault, which is an interrupt too. The instruction counter sees the kernel’s detour to handle the fault, but the program does not.

Tip Out of the box, AMD Zen also overcounts conditional branches, a few in tens of millions, from a speculation optimization known as SpecLockMap. The fix is to set a particular bit in the PMU MSR, which Rewind does automatically as does rr#2034.

In order to rewind history, we need a measurement of time that is reliable and deterministic. Our traditional wall-clock time is unreliable due to the effects of the outside world but we do have a reliable measurement of progress through the instruction stream: the conditional branch counter.

Using the conditional branch counter as a proxy for time turns out to be a relatively decent approximation.

Why do we care about having a “realistic” representation of time?

In a recent development, plenty of programs read the clock and make decisions with it, so the guest’s clock has to be at least somewhat realistic. Under exit time, computing is “free”. A test that checks some work “finishes within 1 s” always passes. If the bug you’re chasing is a timeout, exit time will never reproduce it. 🙃.

Races get skewed too with an unrealistic clock. With exit time, a whole burst of work lands in the same instant, which crowds the threads together, so a race can fire far more often in the VM than it ever would on real hardware.

The closer we can emulate the real world, the more likely we are to reproduce a bug that only happens in the real world. Counter time is a better approximation of the real world than exit time, and it is deterministic, so it is the default clock in Rewind.

Some say time is an illusion. I say it’s a jnz counter.

#127273. Industry News: Give Leftover Mashed Potatoes A Caramelized, Crispy Side With A British-Style Classic

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (579 w)
📖 Baca

Industry News: Give Leftover Mashed Potatoes A Caramelized, Crispy Side With A British-Style Classic

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (579 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foodrepublic

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Not many dishes can compete with mashed potatoes.
  • Recent findings suggest that mashed potatoes fried in butter are part of an English comfort-food classic called bubble and squeak.
  • Recent findings suggest that the potatoes need time to develop that crust.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not many dishes can compete with mashed potatoes. Beyond being the ultimate comfort food, and dare we say, the best preparation of potatoes, it's also super budget-friendly, and any leftovers can be saved and used up later. But let's face it: Nothing beats freshly cooked mashed tots. You could pop leftovers in the microwave or oven to reheat them, but they often come out dry and lackluster. To give them a new lease of life, borrow a tip from the Brits (who know a thing or two about mash) and fry them in butter instead.

Recent findings suggest that mashed potatoes fried in butter are part of an English comfort-food classic called bubble and squeak. The dish is traditionally made from Sunday roast leftovers, with mash and cooked cabbage or other veg shallow-fried in butter, lard, or meat drippings until a crispy brown crust forms. That crust is what brings the leftovers back to life, so it's essential to let it form. This comes down to the Maillard reaction, which occurs when amino acids in the potatoes react with reducing sugars. For that to happen, you only need two things: heat and time.

Recent findings suggest that the potatoes need time to develop that crust. If you drop them into the pan and start stirring them around, they'll warm through, but they won't form a base layer. Instead, pat the mash into an even layer in the pan and cook it undisturbed over medium heat for around five minutes, or until the underside is deeply golden. Then flip it and repeat. You'll hear it sizzle and pop as it fries, which is mentioned to be where the name bubble and squeak originates from.

In restaurants across the country, chefs are swapping high-end dining rooms for cozy neighborhood taverns – not to be confused with bars – serving food that's comforting, hearty, and nostalgic. Much of it looks like standard British pub grub, which makes bubble and squeak a natural fit for those looking to hop on the tavern food trend. It's a great side on its own, but with a few smart upgrades, it can easily become the main event.

Recent findings suggest that since the dish goes so well with butter, you can push it into true gourmet territory by whipping up a compound butter. For reference, this is softened butter mixed with sweet or savory flavorings. It truly couldn't be easier to make, yet delivers a world of flavor. In a nod to the dish's Sunday roast heritage, mix butter with garlic, chives, and horseradish, with a spoonful of English mustard for good measure. When it comes to frying, many chefs also advocate for using lard over butter since the semi-solid pork fat has a higher smoke point, allowing the mash to develop a crispier crust. For the best bubble and squeak, we'd recommend using lard to fry, then melting a knob of the compound butter over the finished dish.

Recent findings suggest that then there's what else can go into the dish. In the spirit of making use of your leftovers, toss in any spare roast meat, bacon, or sausage. Even better, cook the bacon or sausage from scratch in the pan first, remove it, add the butter, and let the potatoes soak up all that flavorful leftover fond. For a cheesy, tangy edge, mix a generous handful of grated cheddar and a spoonful of Dijon mustard into the mash before frying.

It has been revealed that before comparing your balance to anyone else's, you need to know what the benchmarks actually include. Most retirement savings data from Vanguard, Fidelity, and the Federal Reserve covers:.

What these numbers typically exclude: taxable brokerage accounts, real estate equity, HSA balances invested for retirement, pension values, and Social Security. For FI-minded savers, this distinction matters enormously — your total investable net worth is almost certainly larger than your "retirement savings" as defined by these surveys.

Sources indicate that the gap between average and median retirement savings is one of the most important distinctions in personal finance. The average gets pulled upward by high-balance accounts — a single person with $5 million in their 401(k) dramatically inflates the average for their age group. The median (the middle number when all balances are ranked) gives you a far more honest picture of what a typical American actually has saved.

Notice how the gap widens with age. By 65+, the average is 3.3 times the median — meaning a small number of disciplined savers (or high earners) are pulling the average far above what most people actually have. The median tells you what a typical person in each age group actually holds. If you are above the median, you are doing better than half of Americans your age. But "better than average" and "on track for a secure retirement" are very different standards.

Sources indicate that vanguard's annual "How America Saves" report and Fidelity's quarterly retirement analysis provide the most comprehensive snapshots of what Americans hold in their workplace retirement accounts. These numbers reflect defined-contribution plan balances only — primarily 401(k) and 403(b) accounts.

Average balance: $13,265. Median balance: $5,400. Most savers in this bracket have been contributing for fewer than five years. The biggest advantage this group has is time — a 25-year-old contributing $6,000 per year with a 7% average return will accumulate over $1.2 million by age 65 without ever increasing their contribution. The FI community emphasizes that getting started early matters far more than starting with large contributions.

Average balance: $53,300. Median balance: $21,000. This is where employer matches start compounding meaningfully. Fidelity data demonstrates that employees who have been contributing consistently since their 20s have balances 2.5 to 3 times higher than those who started in their 30s. The typical employer match adds 3-6% of salary — effectively free money that many employees still leave on the table. According to Vanguard, roughly 25% of eligible employees do not contribute enough to capture their full employer match.

Average balance: $142,069. Median balance: $60,763. Earnings typically peak in this decade, making it the critical window for aggressive savings. FIRE-path savers in this age bracket commonly have $500,000 to $1 million or more saved by maximizing their 401(k) ($25,500 in 2027), HSA ($4,500 individual / $9,000 family), and Roth IRA ($7,000) — then directing additional savings into taxable brokerage accounts.

Recent findings suggest that fidelity's guideline of 1x salary by 30 and 10x salary by 67 is a reasonable starting point for traditional retirement planning. But for FI seekers, these benchmarks are the floor, not the ceiling. The ChooseFI community consistently demonstrates that saving 40-60% of income — rather than the national average of 4.6% — compresses the timeline from 40 working years down to 10-17.

If your balance is below the median for your age group, you are not alone — and you are not stuck. The math of compound growth means that aggressive action in your 40s and 50s can still produce a secure retirement or even an early one.

The IRS provides additional contribution room for savers age 50 and older. In 2027, the 401(k) catch-up contribution is $7,500 on top of the standard $25,500 limit, for a total of $31,000. IRA catch-up contributions add $1,000 to the standard $7,000 limit. HSA catch-up for those 55+ adds another $1,000. Combined with employer matching, a 50-year-old couple can potentially shelter $80,000 or more per year in tax-advantaged accounts.

Sources indicate that most financial advice focuses on investment returns, but the variable you control most directly is your savings rate. Moving from a 10% savings rate to a 30% savings rate has a dramatically larger impact on your retirement timeline than chasing an extra 2% of investment return. A household earning $120,000 that increases from 10% to 30% savings — a shift of $24,000 per year — adds roughly $600,000 to their retirement balance over 15 years (assuming 7% average returns).

According to recent reports, the FI community's core insight is that savings rate is the primary driver of financial independence. At a 50% savings rate, you can reach FI in roughly 17 years regardless of income level. At 60%, it compresses to about 12 years. At 70%, you are looking at under 10 years. These numbers are independent of salary — they depend only on the ratio of savings to spending.

The average American contributes 4.6% of salary to their 401(k), receives a 3-4% employer match, and saves little outside of that. FIRE-path savers typically max every available tax-advantaged account, maintain savings rates of 40-60%, invest in low-cost index funds, and direct overflow savings into taxable brokerage accounts. The result: FIRE savers in their 40s commonly have $500,000 to $1.5 million in total investable assets — 5 to 10 times the national median for their age group. The difference is not income; many FIRE success stories come from median-income households that simply saved aggressively and avoided lifestyle inflation.

According to recent reports, if you are 40 with $50,000 saved and feeling behind, shifting from a 10% savings rate to a 40% savings rate on a $100,000 income adds $30,000 per year to your investment accounts. At 7% average returns, that alone grows to over $950,000 in 15 years — before counting the $50,000 you already have. Starting late is not ideal, but a high savings rate compresses the timeline dramatically.

In a recent development, the average is pulled upward by a small percentage of very high-balance accounts. If nine people have $10,000 saved and one person has $1,000,000, the average is $109,000 but the median is $10,000. The median gives a far more accurate picture of what a typical American has saved. Yes — employer matching contributions are part of your retirement savings balance. In a typical arrangement, an employer matches 50% of your contributions up to 6% of salary. Retirement planning should focus on investable assets — accounts you can convert to income without selling your primary residence.

A common guideline is 10-12x your pre-retirement income. For a household earning $100,000, that means $1,000,000 to $1,200,000 in retirement savings. The 4% rule suggests you can withdraw 4% of your portfolio annually with a high probability of not running out over 30 years — so $1 million supports roughly $40,000 per year in withdrawals.

Sources indicate that it is never too late, but the urgency increases with age. A 40-year-old saving $20,000 per year at 7% returns will accumulate roughly $1 million by age 65. A 50-year-old has access to catch-up contributions ($7,500 extra in a 401(k)) and can still build $400,000 to $600,000 in 15 years with aggressive saving. The key is maximizing savings rate immediately rather than trying to make up ground through risky investments.

The average retirement savings benchmarks are useful directional guides, but they should not define your target. Most Americans are dramatically undersaved — the median 401(k) balance at retirement age is under $75,000, which supports only about $2,860 per year in withdrawals using the 4% rule. That is not a retirement proposal; it is a supplement to Social Security at best. The FI community takes a fundamentally different approach: define your actual annual spending, multiply by 25, and work backward to a savings rate that gets you there. Whether your number is $750,000 or $3 million, the path is the same — maximize tax-advantaged accounts, invest in low-cost index funds, maintain a high savings rate, and let compound growth do the heavy lifting. If you are behind the benchmarks, the single most impactful action is increasing your savings rate, not chasing higher returns.

When we add another bolognese to the blog (Yes, we already have versions 1, 2, 3, and 4), you know it’s something special! This newest version is made with EGGPLANT, meaning it’s the perfect bolognese for late summer. It’s light yet satisfying, creamy yet bright, and full of bold Italian-inspired flavor — everyone will be asking for seconds!

Industry observers note that even better? It’s a breeze to make — just 1 pot required! What are you waiting for? Get that pasta water boiling!

Industry observers note that bolognese is an Italian sauce that gets its name from the Italian city of Bologna. It’s typically made with meat, soffrito (onions, celery, and carrots), white wine, milk, and tomato paste or sauce, all simmered to create a rich, flavorful sauce.

Industry observers note that our eggplant version strays from the traditional as it excludes meat (and includes eggplant) and incorporates dairy alternatives. But the rest of the dish is very similar to traditional bolognese and feels so hearty it might convert even the most adamant veggie skeptics!

According to recent reports, this 1-pot eggplant bolognese is everything you want for a cozy pasta night, minus the fuss! It starts with sautéing onion and carrots to create a simple, savory-sweet base. Next, we add eggplant (cut into very small cubes) and let it sauté until it has softened and browned (hello, flavor!).

Recent findings suggest that build the flavor even further with garlic and red pepper flakes and by deglazing the pan with wine. Crushed tomatoes and tomato paste ensure a bright, tomato-forward sauce, and a small amount of dairy-free milk (we like homemade cashew milk) gives it a gentle creaminess and richness. The final flavor touches include dried Italian herbs (basil + oregano), sea salt, and maple syrup to balance the acidity of the tomatoes.

In a recent development, once all the ingredients are in your pan, it’s time to let the heat do its magic. Simmering for at least 20-30 minutes allows the sauce to thicken and concentrates the flavors as liquid evaporates away. If you have the time, you can let it continue simmering for up to an hour for even more flavor!

It has been revealed that when it’s done simmering, you’ll be left with an oh-so delicious, plant-powered sauce perfect for serving with your favorite pasta! It would also be lovely over polenta and is elevated by garnishing with fresh basil and our homemade vegan parmesan cheese.

Recent findings suggest that we think you’ll LOVE this eggplant bolognese! It’s:RichSavoryCreamy yet brightLight yet satisfyingEasy to make& SO delicious!

It’s the perfect dish for a late summer pasta night! While quick enough for a weeknight, it’s also impressive enough to serve to dinner guests, especially paired with our Simple Vegan Meatballs, Pesto Turkey Meatballs, or Chickpea Caesar Salad (30 Minutes!).

Sources indicate that everything you love about enchiladas, minus the fuss! This super flavorful, cheesy vegan enchilada skillet comes together in about 30 minutes with simple methods, minimal dishes, and no need to fill or roll tortillas.

It has been revealed that this easy, nourishing dish features tender cubed sweet potato or winter squash, fiber- & protein-rich black beans, and a rich red enchilada sauce. Everything gets simmered in 1 pan and topped with a melty cashew “cheese” that makes it SUPER satisfying and delicious!

It’s believed that enchiladas may have originated from a similar Mayan dish called papadzules. But the first written recipe for enchiladas was in an 1831 cookbook called El Cocinero mexicano. Typically, enchiladas are made with meat, seafood, beans, cheese, potatoes, or vegetables stuffed in corn tortillas and topped with enchilada sauce.

Our “inspired-by” enchilada skillet has all the flavors of classic enchiladas, but it’s vegan, and instead of rolling the filling in tortillas, we slice the tortillas and cook everything together in one pan on the stovetop!

It has been revealed that this 1-pan, 30-minute vegan enchilada skillet begins with a base of sautéed vegetables — onion, garlic, sweet potato, and poblano pepper. The veggies are flexible here, so feel free to experiment! We love kabocha squash for a fall variation and have found green bell peppers work well when poblanos aren’t available. We also think butternut squash would be nice, as would greens such as kale or spinach.

Once the onions are very tender and the squash and peppers are just beginning to soften, we stir in black beans + corn tortillas that have been sliced into strips.

In a recent development, next comes the final ingredient in the skillet portion of this dish (hello, simple + flavorful!): red enchilada sauce. We love the bold flavor of our homemade enchilada sauce (and usually have it stocked in the freezer), but this recipe also works well with store-bought enchilada sauce.

And lastly, it just wouldn’t be enchiladas without: the CHEESE! More specifically, a flavorful cashew “cheese” sauce inspired by our fan favorite Cheesy Vegan Pizza Beans. It’s made by blending up cashews, water, lime juice, garlic, tapioca starch, and sea salt. When poured over the enchilada skillet and covered with a lid, the heat and tapioca starch do their magic, creating a melty, cheesy layer! Total swoon!

We highly recommend trying the cashew “cheese” sauce, even if you’re not vegan or dairy-free! It’s super easy and takes this dish to a whole latest level. However, this enchilada skillet is also delicious with shredded vegan or dairy cheese (such as pepper jack).

  • What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?
  • Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

What draws someone to another person when they’re already in a committed relationship?

Both positive and dark personality traits are linked to becoming infatuated with someone outside a committed relationship.

The clearest link among the dark traits is with psychopathy, which includes impulsivity and a lack of empathy.

Yet a more positive trait, the tendency to see value in other people and admire their qualities, is also linked to stronger infatuation once other differences are taken into account.

The researchers suggest that impulsivity may make a upcoming attraction more rewarding, while an appreciation of other people may make it easier to form an emotional connection with them.

People who are more open to casual sex or less satisfied with their relationship also report stronger feelings for someone else.

The study involved just over 300 adults in Romania who were in committed relationships.

They completed questionnaires about their personality, their attitudes and experiences around casual sex, and how satisfied they were with their relationship.

The researchers also asked about the thoughts, feelings and desires people had towards someone other than their partner.

Psychologists call this extradyadic infatuation, a preoccupation that can involve repeatedly thinking about someone and feeling unable to tell your partner how strongly you feel.

People who scored higher on humanism, the tendency to value and admire others, generally reported less infatuation outside their relationship.

Of all the factors the researchers examined, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation after the others were taken into account.

The researchers suggest that people high in humanism may be more receptive to forming a close connection with someone new.

Faith in humanity, which reflects a belief in other people’s goodwill, highlighted a different pattern and remained linked to less infatuation.

People who expect others to be dependable may also see their existing relationship as more secure and feel less drawn to alternatives, the researchers suggest.

Machiavellianism, a tendency to approach relationships strategically and manipulate others for personal gain, also showed a reversal.

It was linked to stronger infatuation when examined on its own and to weaker infatuation once the other factors were considered.

The researchers suggest that someone who takes a calculating approach to relationships may be wary of an outside attachment that demands sustained emotional investment.

Psychopathic traits, by comparison, were linked to stronger infatuation in both analyses.

When the researchers compared all the factors together, openness to casual sex had the strongest link to infatuation.

Dissatisfaction with an existing relationship may also make an alternative partner seem more appealing, although the survey leaves open whether dissatisfaction precedes the infatuation or follows it.

The study was published in the journal Psychological Reports (Huţanu & Holman, 2026).

Tech Report: What is EMDR therapy, and does it actually work?

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1703 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr.
  • It has been revealed that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years.
  • Recent findings suggest that if you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that clinically reviewed by Dr. Chris Mosunic, PhD, RD, MBA.

It has been revealed that maybe a friend swears EMDR helped her move past something she’d carried for years. Or maybe you came across it online while searching for ways to cope with a memory that still feels heavy. Whether you’ve heard of EMDR but don’t know how it works, or you’re familiar with the approach but skeptical, we’re here to break it all down.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re uncertain, that’s understandable, because EMDR can sound unconventional: you briefly recall a painful memory while following side-to-side stimulation, like tracking a moving target with your eyes. But the research tells a more reassuring story. It’s a well-studied therapy for trauma, and it’s increasingly explored for anxiety and depression, too.

Here’s what EMDR involves, what the research shows, and what a session is like, so you have a clearer picture of whether it might make sense for you.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a structured therapy that helps the brain reprocess distressing memories so they carry less emotional weight. Psychologist Francine Shapiro, PhD, developed it in the late 1980s after she noticed that certain eye movements seemed to ease her own troubling thoughts.

EMDR rests on Shapiro’s adaptive information processing model. The idea is that your brain normally files an experience away, so you can recall it later without feeling like you’re living it again. But a frightening or painful event can interrupt that process, leaving the memory raw and unfiled, still carrying the fear and detail of that moment. That’s why it can resurface later, as vivid as the day it happened.

It has been revealed that according to this model, “processing” a memory means helping your brain finish the filing. You don’t forget what happened, and the facts don’t change. What changes is the emotional charge it carries, so recalling it feels less like reliving it and more like remembering it. To help that happen, EMDR uses a technique called “bilateral stimulation.”.

EMDR uses a technique called bilateral stimulation. While you hold a difficult memory in mind, a trained therapist guides you through side-to-side stimulation.

Bilateral stimulation can take a few forms:.

eye movements that follow your therapist’s fingers.

gentle taps that switch between your hands or knees.

tones that play in one ear, then the other.

According to recent reports, there’s a theory behind the side-to-side part, though researchers are still working out exactly why it helps. The leading explanation is about mental bandwidth. Your working memory, the part of your mind that holds what you’re focused on right now, can only handle so much at once. When you track side-to-side movement while recalling a hard memory, the two tasks compete for that limited space. The hard memory tends to feel a little less vivid, and with repetition it can lose its sharp edges, so it feels less overwhelming to hold.

💙 Learn more in our guide to bilateral stimulation.

Sources indicate that EMDR has eight phases, though they tend to blend together in practice. The early phases cover your history and teach you coping skills, so you feel prepared before any hard memories arise. In the middle phases, you focus on a specific memory while following bilateral stimulation, which is meant to help your brain reprocess it. The final phases check that the memory feels less distressing and help you close out the work safely.

Sources indicate that the evidence is strong for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), a condition that can develop after a frightening or life-threatening event. A Cochrane review (a gold-standard summary of research on a topic) found that EMDR and trauma-focused cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) both reduce PTSD symptoms. They also outperformed other therapies when researchers checked in after treatment ended. A 2024 review in the Journal of Traumatic Stress identified more than 30 randomized controlled trials supporting EMDR for PTSD in adults and children. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, recommend EMDR for PTSD.

Industry observers note that however, some guidelines, including those from the American Psychological Association (APA), rate the evidence for EMDR as less certain than for trauma-focused CBT. Researchers also debate exactly why EMDR works.

💙 Read more about how EMDR can help you cope with PTSD.

Recent findings suggest that the picture is more mixed outside PTSD. Early research suggests EMDR may help with anxiety, as one meta-analysis found reduced symptoms of anxiety, panic, and phobia, though the studies were small and varied in quality.

According to recent reports, evidence for depression is emerging as well. Another meta-analysis showed reduced depression symptoms, with the strongest effects in more severe cases. These findings are promising, but they don’t carry the same weight as the PTSD research.

After you and a therapist finish the early phases, you bring a specific memory to mind and notice the thoughts and body sensations that come with it. Then your therapist guides you through the bilateral stimulation while you let your mind go where it goes. You can ask to pause or stop at any time. Unlike many talk therapies, EMDR doesn’t require you to describe the memory in detail.

According to recent reports, sessions usually run 60–90 minutes. Your therapist pauses often to check in on what you noticed. Over several rounds of bilateral stimulation, many people find the memory feels less sharp, even though the facts don’t change. Between sessions, a mindfulness practice, such as slow breathing or a body scan, can help you ease feelings that surface.

According to recent reports, 💙 Explore Calm's EMDR-Inspired Bilateral: Anxiety, a set of music tracks that alternate gently between your left and right ear. It draws on the bilateral stimulation used in EMDR, though audio-only versions haven’t been studied on their own the way clinical EMDR has. Think of it as a calming complement to therapy, not a replacement for a trained therapist.

Sources indicate that the answer varies, since it depends on what you’re working through. For a single, recent trauma, some people notice their symptoms ease within a handful of sessions. More complex or long-standing trauma usually takes longer, sometimes many months. Therapists describe a typical course as 6–12 sessions, though it varies widely from person to person.

Industry observers note that along the way, some people feel worse before they feel better. Painful memories can stir up strong emotions in the short term, which is common and doesn’t mean EMDR isn’t working. Before reprocessing begins, your therapist teaches you coping skills, such as grounding exercises that anchor you in the present, so you have tools to use if those feelings get intense.

Industry observers note that 💙 Try the 5, 4, 3, 2, 1 practice, a quick way to ground yourself in the present, with Prof. Megan Reitz.

EMDR stands for eye movement desensitization and reprocessing. It’s a form of therapy that uses bilateral stimulation, such as guided eye movements, to help your brain process distressing memories so they feel less intense. Psychologist Francine Shapiro developed this therapy in the late 1980s.

Recent findings suggest that EMDR may help with anxiety, though PTSD is where the evidence is strongest. The studies on anxiety are smaller and less consistent. If your anxiety is tied to a specific frightening experience, it may be worth asking a therapist whether EMDR fits your situation.

💙 Explore how mindfulness can help you manage your anxiety.

EMDR differs from talk therapy because it doesn’t require you to describe your experience in detail. You’ll still talk with your therapist, especially early on, but the reprocessing happens while you hold a memory in mind and follow bilateral stimulation. Talk therapies like cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) focus more on examining and reshaping your thoughts out loud.

The main benefit of EMDR is that it can ease the distress tied to painful memories. For many people with PTSD, that can mean fewer flashbacks and less of that constant, on-alert feeling.

It has been revealed that much of the debate is about why EMDR works, not whether it does. The evidence is strongest for PTSD, with early and more mixed findings for anxiety and depression.

Recent findings suggest that some studies suggest the eye movements themselves add little. The benefit may instead come from giving your mind a second task while you recall a memory, which can make it feel less vivid and emotionally intense. Other tasks that split your attention may have the same effect.

Certain guidelines, including the APA’s, consider the evidence for EMDR less established than for trauma-focused CBT. None of this takes away from the relief many people find with EMDR. It’s useful context as you weigh your options with a therapist.

EMDR is generally safe when a trained therapist delivers it, though you may experience some short-term effects. You might feel more emotional or tired between sessions, or have vivid dreams as your brain keeps processing the memory.

Industry observers note that these reactions usually pass within a day or two. If they last longer or feel overwhelming, it’s a good idea to tell your therapist, who can adjust the pace with you. Serious side effects are uncommon when a therapist follows the full eight-phase process.

The number of sessions you need depends on the memory you’re addressing and how long it has affected you. Some people feel relief after a few sessions, while longer-standing experiences often take more time. A common range is 6–12 sessions, but your timeline may be shorter or longer. Your therapist can give you a better sense of what to expect once they know your history.

Full EMDR needs a trained therapist, so it’s not something to try on your own. A therapist helps you reprocess memories and stay grounded if one feels overwhelming, which matters most with intense trauma.

#127249. Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (787 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Coffee doesn’t have to keep you awake to disrupt your sleep

📅 22 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (787 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep.
  • To investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity.
  • Industry observers note that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, for years, people have debated whether drinking coffee in the evening interferes with sleep. Some people can have caffeine late in the day and fall asleep easily, while others may remain awake for hours. But researchers are increasingly finding that simply asking whether coffee delays sleep may miss a more vital concern: what caffeine does to the brain after sleep begins.

To investigate those effects, scientists are using EEG, or electroencephalography -- a method used to record the brain's electrical activity. EEG measurements can reveal much more than how long someone sleeps or how often they wake up. They can also provide clues about the biological quality and depth of that sleep.

Industry observers note that "EEG allows us to see not only whether a person is sleeping, but also how the brain is sleeping. Classical sleep assessment assesses sleep duration and its stages, whereas quantitative EEG analysis reveals more subtle changes, such as reduced slow-wave activity, which is an key marker of sleep depth and its restorative character," explains Prof. Donata Kurpas from the Department of Nursing, Wroclaw Medical University.

Slow waves are a major feature of deep sleep -- the stage associated with physical recovery, replenishing energy reserves, and maintaining healthy brain function.

Caffeine May Make Sleep Less Restorative.

Industry observers note that caffeine does not always affect sleep in obvious ways. A person may still fall asleep at a normal time and remain asleep for what appears to be a full night, yet the quality of that rest may still be altered.

"Caffeine may shorten sleep or make it more difficult to fall asleep; however, even when sleep duration appears normal, it may reduce slow-wave activity and shift the EEG pattern toward a more 'wakeful' brain," says Prof. Kurpas.

According to recent reports, in practical terms, someone might spend eight hours in bed without getting the same level of neurological recovery they would normally expect. Because the disruption may not cause obvious awakenings, it can easily go unnoticed.

In a recent development, "The subjective feeling of having slept well does not always correspond to what we observe in neurophysiological recordings. A person may fall asleep without major difficulty and not remember awakenings, while the brain may display fewer features of deep sleep," the expert adds.

Why Caffeine Affects People Differently.

Another major finding from caffeine research is that responses vary considerably from person to person. Genetics, metabolism, age, stress, and chronic fatigue can all influence how strongly caffeine affects sleep.

For some people, even coffee consumed early in the day may still have an impact by nighttime.

"It is not only about coffee consumed just before bedtime. For some people, the total amount of caffeine consumed during the day and whether the body has enough time to metabolize it before nightfall may also be crucial," Prof. Kurpas emphasizes.

That possibility may be especially relevant for people who rely on caffeine to improve focus, stamina, or performance, including athletes, people doing mentally demanding work, and anyone who regularly uses coffee or other caffeinated products to stay alert.

Caffeine Can Create a Fatigue Cycle.

Recent findings suggest that caffeine can temporarily increase alertness and make fatigue feel less noticeable. However, experts caution that the boost may sometimes come at the expense of the body's ability to recover fully during sleep.

Industry observers note that in that sense, caffeine can resemble "borrowing energy" from the body. If nighttime recovery becomes less effective, the person may feel more tired the following day and turn to even more caffeine for help.

Sources indicate that "If caffeine helps a person function during the day while simultaneously worsening the quality of nighttime recovery, a vicious circle may develop: greater fatigue, greater need for stimulation, and poorer sleep," says Prof. Kurpas.

According to recent reports, these findings are one reason sleep researchers are paying less attention to sleep duration alone. Increasingly, the focus is shifting toward what the brain is actually doing during the night and whether that sleep is biologically restorative.

Sources indicate that "Caffeine is neither 'good' nor 'bad'. It is a biologically active substance whose effects depend on dose, time of day, age, lifestyle, sleep quality, stress burden, and individual sensitivity," the expert concludes.

#127248. Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1435 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Calm ↗ Open Full Page

Can you be friends with your ex? What to consider first

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Calm

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago.
  • In a recent development, moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing.
  • Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your phone buzzes. It’s your ex, sending a meme you would’ve laughed at together six months ago. You smile, then wonder why you smiled.

In a recent development, moments like this are why staying friends with an ex can feel so confusing. For some people, staying connected feels natural because the habit, and maybe the care, is still there. For others, it makes healing feel harder. Every situation is different, and you’re allowed to take your time figuring out what works for you.

Whether you’re the one hoping to stay in touch or the one being asked to, here’s how to tell if staying friends would help you move on or make it harder.

According to recent reports, in some cases, you may be able to. Post-breakup friendships can be healthy and meaningful when the breakup was mutual, the relationship had little conflict, and both people have had time to grieve.

That noted, every friendship between exes is different. Researchers who study friendships after breakups describe two kinds. In one, both people have moved on and value the connection. In the other, one or both people stay in touch because of lingering attraction or reluctance to end things. The first kind can be rewarding. The second can make it harder to get over the breakup.

The dynamic you had with your ex matters, too. A study found that relationships shaped by high conflict, emotional dependency, or attachment anxiety may be harder to turn into a friendship afterward.

Before you decide anything, it may help to reflect on why you want to stay in touch. A few questions to sit with:.

What am I hoping this friendship gives me?

Am I trying to stay close to them or avoid the discomfort of letting go?

How would I feel if they started dating someone new?

If the last question stings, it may just mean that you need more time.

Recent findings suggest that if you were the one who ended things, you might want friendship out of guilt or a wish to soften the loss. If you were the one who was left, you might view friendship as a potential path to getting back together.

Industry observers note that if the answers don’t come right away, try a mindfulness practice. A few minutes of reflection or a short breathing exercise can help you sort through what you’re thinking and feeling.

💙 Try the Pause to Check In meditation on the Calm app.

Industry observers note that if you’ve thought it through and still want to stay in touch, a few signs suggest a friendship may work. People who are securely attached often find it easier to stay friends after a breakup, but the list below can apply to anyone:.

You both see the breakup as mutual, with no ongoing hurt, resentment, or blame.

You’ve both accepted that the romantic relationship is over, with no unresolved romantic feelings.

There’s a reason for the friendship beyond comfort or familiarity, such as shared values, kids together, or a work connection.

In certain cases, staying friends can make healing harder or keep you from pouring energy into new parts of your life:.

You’re still in love with your ex and hoping the friendship leads somewhere.

The relationship involved emotional manipulation, control, or abuse.

The friendship gets in the way of new relationships, like when a new partner feels uneasy about your connection.

You have different expectations for the friendship, which could leave one of you hurt.

💙 Discover the signs of having a toxic ex.

It can be, especially since staying in touch can make it harder to let go. One study found that regular contact with an ex may slow emotional recovery. When you’re still part of each other’s routines, it can be harder to mourn the end of the relationship.

By contrast, a low-contact friendship, where you talk occasionally and keep to limits you’ve agreed on, is less likely to hold either of you back.

Sources indicate that how you feel after you talk is worth paying attention to. If you often feel sad, anxious, or unsettled, or you keep replaying the conversation, it may help to take some space.

💙 Read more on how to deal with a breakup when you’re hurting.

Recent findings suggest that it may be appropriate to be friends with your ex, depending on your situation. It tends to work best when you’ve both moved on, the breakup didn’t involve harm, and the friendship fits both of your lives. If it also feels honest and comfortable to you, that’s a good sign.

Sources indicate that being friends with an ex isn’t automatically a red flag. If your partner is friends with an ex, how they handle it matters more than the friendship itself. A few questions to consider:.

Transparency: Do they talk about it openly, or does it feel secretive?

Priorities: Do they make time for you and the relationship?

Boundaries: Are there clear limits on the friendship, or does contact feel constant and undefined?

Responsiveness: When you raise a concern, does your partner listen or dismiss it?

If something doesn’t sit right, you could bring it up and see whether they listen, get defensive, or brush you off. If you’re the one staying friends with an ex, your new partner’s concerns are worth hearing out, even if nothing is wrong.

You don’t have to keep in touch with your ex after a breakup. Taking space is often healthy and necessary, and you can change your mind later. You can choose a full break, a time-limited break (“let’s not talk for a few months”), or a low-contact friendship.

If you do stay in touch, some boundaries may protect your well-being. A few to consider:.

Set a pace. Daily texting can pull you back into old routines, so try starting with occasional check-ins instead.

Decide what’s off limits. That might mean dating lives, old conflicts, and late-night “remember when” talks.

In a recent development, give yourself space online. Mute or unfollow for a while to adjust without ending the connection.

Industry observers note that blueprint a review and a way out. After a few months, ask whether the friendship still feels good. If it doesn’t, have a line ready, like “I think I need to take a step back for now.”.

If you share children, a workplace, or a friend group, you may need to stay in touch. It’s often best to stick to logistics, like pickup times for the kids or project deadlines at work.

💙 Explore the Boundaries meditation on Calm.

There’s no set amount of time to wait before trying to be friends with an ex. Some people feel ready within months, while others take years. Some never feel ready or choose not to be friends, and that’s okay.

It has been revealed that A question to ask yourself is whether you can feel okay about the thought of your ex moving on. If that still hurts, you probably need more time.

It has been revealed that yes, being friends with an ex can sometimes turn into getting back together. Whether that’s a good thing depends on why your relationship ended and whether those reasons have changed.

Problems tied to circumstances, like bad timing or distance, may be easier to work through than core differences, like values, long-term goals, or how you communicate. If you get back together and those core differences haven’t changed, the same patterns can resurface.

It’s painful when one of you wants to stay friends after a breakup and the other doesn’t, and what helps depends on which side you’re on.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re the one being asked, you’re allowed to say “not yet” or “no.” If you’re unsure, you don’t have to answer right away. You might say:.

“I care about you, and I need some time before I know what this looks like.”.

“Can we revisit this in a few months?”.

“I’m not able to be friends right now, and I hope you can respect that.”.

If you’re the one who wants friendship, the kindest move is to respect the space your ex has asked for. If you push for contact, it can get harder for you both to move on, even if giving them room hurts.

#127247. When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (686 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable

📅 24 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense.
  • Industry observers note that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R.
  • The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that sometimes what we see does not immediately make sense. A shadow can briefly resemble a face, or one object can momentarily be mistaken for another. Upcoming research suggests that the brain may resolve these visual conflicts by allowing different regions to compare their interpretations until a more consistent picture emerges.

Industry observers note that in a study published in Nature Neuroscience, Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory Cynthia R. Stebbins Fellow Mitra Javadzadeh and collaborators at the University of Cambridge and University College London examined how two neighboring regions of the visual cortex interact. They found that when activity in the two regions matched, the shared pattern persisted. When the regions produced conflicting patterns, however, the disagreement faded within a fraction of a second.

The findings offer a possible explanation for how the brain combines information from specialized regions into a single, coherent perception.

How Specialized Brain Regions Work Together.

According to recent reports, different parts of the brain are responsible for processing different streams of sensory information, yet our experience of the world usually feels unified rather than fragmented. Understanding how those specialized systems coordinate with one another is a major challenge in neuroscience.

"We are trying to understand how you can have such a high level of specialization between these different blocks, yet always have a consistent holistic outcome," Javadzadeh says.

Industry observers note that the researchers focused on two well known visual processing regions in the brain's neocortex: the primary visual cortex (V1) and the lateromedial visual area (LM). Visual processing does not simply move in one direction from one region to the next. Instead, these areas continually exchange information with each other.

Testing What Happens When Visual Areas Disagree.

It has been revealed that to explore that communication, Javadzadeh and her colleagues trained mice to tell the difference between two visual patterns tilted in opposite directions. The animals received a reward for recognizing only one of the orientations.

During the task, the researchers temporarily silenced either V1 or LM and watched how the remaining region behaved without its usual partner. The team then used those observations to create an artificial neural network model of the V1-LM circuit. With that model, they could test how the system might respond when particular neurons were altered.

Industry observers note that the results revealed a striking pattern. Activity that conflicted between the two brain regions promptly disappeared, while activity shared by both areas lasted longer.

"We find that over time, these types of connections between areas implement a mechanism we call consensus building," Javadzadeh explains.

A Possible Brainwide Consensus Mechanism.

The study examined only two regions involved in vision, but the researchers are now investigating whether the same process may operate more broadly across the neocortex.

"For example, when what you see contradicts with what you hear, do you still use the same kind of mechanisms to reconcile these two?" she wonders.

It has been revealed that if dynamic consensus building turns out to be widespread, it could help scientists better understand how the brain combines competing signals into a stable interpretation of the world. It could also shed light on what happens when different brain regions fail to arrive at the same conclusion.

The idea may even have implications beyond neuroscience. Similar principles could help researchers think about how artificial intelligence systems might handle conflicting streams of information and decide which signals to trust.

Industry observers note that "While we understand individual building blocks of the brain, what is the glue that puts them together?" Javadzadeh asks. "Knowing that can finally help us understand how the brain works as a whole.".

#127246. Latest Update: The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (593 w)

Latest Update: The Depression And Bladder Medicines That May Increase Dementia Risk

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Org

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.
  • Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

The more of these medications people were prescribed, the higher their rate of dementia diagnosis.

Anticholinergic drugs have been linked to a higher risk of dementia.

These drugs block the action of acetylcholine, a chemical messenger in the brain and body, and are used to treat depression, overactive bladder and symptoms of Parkinson’s disease.

For example, amitriptyline is an antidepressant formerly sold as Tryptizol in the UK and Elavil in the US.

Oxybutynin, used to treat overactive bladder, also has anticholinergic effects and comes in patches known as Kentera in the UK and Oxytrol in the US.

In a study of more than 217,000 people, each additional anticholinergic medicine prescribed at the start was associated with a 15 per cent higher rate of dementia diagnosis in the UK group and about a 6 per cent higher rate in the US group.

Acetylcholine helps the brain pay attention, learn and form memories.

In the bladder, blocking certain acetylcholine signals can help control involuntary contractions.

Blocking those signals in the brain can make it harder to concentrate and may cause confusion.

Other tricyclic antidepressants with anticholinergic effects include clomipramine, known by the brand name Anafranil in both countries, and nortriptyline, known as Allegron in the UK and Pamelor in the US.

Paroxetine, an SSRI antidepressant with anticholinergic effects, has been sold as Seroxat in the UK and Paxil in the US.

Some antipsychotics also have these effects, including olanzapine, known as Zyprexa in both countries and used to treat schizophrenia and bipolar disorder.

The medicines have different uses, which makes their shared effect easy to overlook when someone takes several prescriptions for unrelated conditions.

Using a list of 88 medicines, the researchers counted how many each person had been prescribed at the start of the study.

They then looked at dementia diagnoses over a median of about 16 years in the UK Biobank and nine years in the US All of Us Research Program.

About a quarter of participants in the British group and just over a fifth of those in the American group had been prescribed at least one medicine on the list.

The increases were relative, and fewer than two in 100 participants in each group were diagnosed with dementia during follow-up.

The percentages describe how the rate of dementia diagnosis varied with the number of medicines prescribed and give no risk estimate for any individual drug.

A prescription can reveal something about a person’s health as well as what medicine they have been given.

Depression and Parkinson’s disease, for example, can lead to anticholinergic prescribing and are themselves associated with dementia risk.

The researchers could account for some differences in health between participants, but the reasons for prescribing and the severity of those conditions could still explain part of the association.

A count taken at the start also gives only a snapshot, since people may change medicines or stop taking them over the years.

For someone taking several prescriptions, a prescriber or pharmacist can review the full list and weigh the benefits and risks of each medicine in context.

The study was published in the journal Age and Ageing (Asiimwe et al., 2025).
