📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A neuroimaging study reveals that women who chronically view their own appearance from an outsider’s perspective, a psychological trait known as self-objectification, exhibit dampened brain activity in aesthetic judgment regions when viewing sexualized images of women. The findings suggest that internalized beauty standards reshape how the brain regulates and evaluates objectifying media.

Source: Society for Neuroscience.

Widespread sexualization of women across advertising, entertainment, and social media has long been linked to societal objectification and broad mental health burdens, including body dissatisfaction, anxiety, and disordered eating.

Over time, repeated exposure to objectifying imagery can lead individuals to internalize an observer’s gaze, a psychological phenomenon known as self-objectification, in which a person habitually monitors and evaluates their own body from an outsider’s perspective.

While behavioral studies have established that self-objectification heightens sensitivity to media portrayals, precisely how a woman’s self-perception alters the underlying neural circuitry that evaluates sexualized visuals has remained unclear.

In a study published today in eNeuro, a research team led by Zhennan Liu at Shanghai Normal University and Haoyue Qian at the Chinese Academy of Sciences investigated how individual differences in self-objectification shape both subjective beauty judgments and brain responses to sexualized imagery.

Recent findings suggest that the investigators recruited 60 healthy cisgender heterosexual female participants with an average age of approximately 20 years. First, the team assessed each participant’s baseline level of self-objectification using a validated psychological scale measuring how strongly individuals prioritize external appearance over internal bodily competence.

Next, participants viewed and rated a series of photographs categorized by the researchers as either:.

While participants across the board rated the sexualized photographs as more attractive than the non-sexualized images, women with higher self-objectification scores assigned significantly higher attractiveness ratings to the sexualized visuals.

When the team examined the accompanying brain activity, they uncovered a striking neural signature: women who scored higher on self-objectification exhibited dampened neural activity in brain regions involved in aesthetic judgment while assessing sexualized images.

Rather than heightened analytical engagement, this reduced activation suggests an altered regulatory or automatic evaluative response when processing culturally idealized, objectifying imagery.

“Differences between individuals [in this study] may come from how their brains regulate and evaluate the attractiveness of these images,” explained Qian.

By connecting self-objectification to measurable shifts in aesthetic evaluation circuitry, the study illustrates how internalized social standards leave a functional footprint on visual and emotional processing.

Looking ahead, the researchers aim to move beyond observational associations to test whether psychological training can buffer the brain against objectifying media.

Sources indicate that “We want to test whether experimentally training or manipulating regulation strategies (e.g., cognitive reappraisal) can change how women respond to and rate sexualized images,” Qian stated. “This will help move the work from association toward causal and intervention-relevant questions.”.

What is “self-objectification,” and how did researchers measure it?

Self-objectification is the tendency to view and judge one’s own body primarily from an outside observer’s perspective, prioritizing physical appearance over internal physical capabilities. Researchers measured this trait using a validated psychological questionnaire before participants viewed media images.

How did self-objectification affect brain responses to sexualized images?

Women with higher self-objectification scores rated sexualized images of women as significantly more attractive than peers with lower scores, and demonstrated dampened brain activity in regions responsible for aesthetic judgment, indicating differences in how their brains regulate and evaluate beauty standards.

Could psychological strategies change how the brain reacts to objectifying media?

Researchers hope to test whether training cognitive regulation techniques, such as cognitive reappraisal, which helps people consciously reframe how they interpret visual stimuli, can modify brain activity and reduce vulnerability to sexualized media representations.

Trait Self-Objectification Modulates Attractiveness-Regulating Neural Activity in Sexual Objectification Processing: An ERP Study.

Industry observers note that contemporary mass media frequently emphasize women’s sexual attractiveness, thereby perpetuating sexual objectification and exacerbating mental distress. Trait self-objectification is presumed to be a risk factor for these adverse outcomes; however, the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying individuals’ responses to sexual objectification remain poorly understood.

The present study examined how trait self-objectification modulates behavioral and electrophysiological responses to sexualized female images. Behaviorally, sexualized portrayals of women increased attractiveness ratings, and this enhancement was further modulated by individual levels of trait self-objectification. Neurally, processing sexualized female images evoked a set of ERPs indexing early neurocognitive processes, including perception-related N170 and EPN, and attention-related P200.

Distinct later neural responses were also identified, including the emotion-related centro-parietal LPP and the regulation-related frontal LPP (f-LPP). Among these sexual objectification-related ERP components, only the f-LPP was modulated by trait self-objectification.

Furthermore, follow-up analyses revealed that the degree to which trait self-objectification increased individuals’ attractiveness ratings of sexualized images was associated with their reduced f-LPP activity.

Collectively, these findings suggest that trait self-objectification modulates the processing of sexually objectifying stimuli by altering neurocognitive processes underlying attractiveness regulation, highlighting the importance of this regulatory mechanism in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

The cultural emphasis on women’s sexual attractiveness perpetuates sexual objectification, which is associated with adverse mental health outcomes. Trait self-objectification may modulate these outcomes, yet its relationship with the processing of sexual objectification remains unclear. This study found that trait self-objectification shapes attractiveness ratings during sexual objectification processing.

Sources indicate that although sexualized images elicited multiple neurocognitive components—N170 and EPN (perception-related), P200 (attention-related), cp-LPP (emotion-related), and f-LPP (regulation-related)—individual differences in trait self-objectification were selectively associated with f-LPP activity. These findings highlight the potential role of attractiveness-related regulatory processing in shaping individual responses to sexual objectification.

How Do You Raise Kids to Be Emotionally Mature?

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting.
  • While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.
  • According to recent reports, according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Raising a teen is one of the last chapters in parenting. During these years, it’s easy to prioritize your child’s grades, sports, and other accolades, especially as they inch toward leaving the nest.

While achievement is one marker of success, there’s another (often overlooked) skill that shapes your teen’s well-being and development: emotional maturity.

According to recent reports, according to clinical psychologist Lindsay Gibson, emotional maturity develops through deep emotional connections, beginning with a child’s parents and primary caretakers. Research indicates emotional maturity is the ability to accept and express care, temper big feelings, and make wise choices. Without it, teens are more likely to feel lonely and less satisfied with life, one study found.

In her latest book, How to Raise an Emotionally Mature Child, Gibson points out that “the quality of humanity’s future depends on the emotional maturity of coming generations.”.

Juli Fraga: In your book, you mention that humanity’s future will depend on emotional maturity. Why does this matter so much right now?

Lindsay Gibson: Emotional maturity is critical to our well-being as individuals and to the smooth, productive, and innovative aspects of society. When you’re emotionally mature, you can think and anticipate consequences. You can also look back and learn from what you’ve done before. So, you can rely on your thinking to help you deal with reality. Emotional maturity also means tuning into your inner world, including your emotions, imagination, hopes, dreams, connections to other people, and sense of belonging.

Sources indicate that JF: Our society places a lot of emphasis on achievement, and less importance on emotional intelligence. How can parents help their teens balance the two?

LG: There’s a real cultural pull in society to prize intelligence and achievement. But when parents get too fixated on these qualities, a child may feel like performance matters more than their thoughts, feelings, and sense of safety.

According to recent reports, kids need to be safely held and supported through the growing-up process. It helps them feel resilient, secure, and confident—qualities they need to take out into the world to function independently. If you get too fixated on the intelligence and achievement parts, you’ve got someone who’s very powerful in one area, but whose emotional side may be underdeveloped. It’s the balance between the two that matters.

According to recent reports, JF: In your book, you mention why it’s so crucial for parents to help their kids develop a sense of self. Can you explain why this matters, especially during the teen years when kids are individuating?

Industry observers note that LG: One way teens find out who they are is by discovering who they’re not. Teens might push a limit or break a rule, and it’s all par for the course. What’s important for parents is to be able to recognize and imagine that their child has a separate heart and mind from theirs—a process called “mentalization.”.

According to recent reports, A self is that inner spark that speaks to us. It indicates “don’t do that” or “now’s the time to go for it.” It guides you toward what’s most compatible with your individuality and who you are meant to be.

Our sense of self comes from our relationships with people we love and who love us. To feel secure, kids need solid, dependable, connected, and deeply resonant relationships with their parents and caretakers. They need parents who are curious and reflect something back that’s meaningful about who the young person is. When they have that foundation, they have a sense of being a real person inside.

In a recent development, JF: Parents are so busy these days, and overloaded—mentally and emotionally. Raising emotionally mature kids may feel like another big to-do on an already long list. What advice do you have?

LG: Taking time to pause and take your child seriously as a real person will work wonders for their self-confidence and future resilience.

Slowing down takes practice because by the time you’re old enough to have a family, you’ve probably been very goal-directed; parents can be pretty hard on themselves because our culture is so fixated on achievement.

But pulling yourself away from your goal for even a second to tend to your child is something worth practicing because that’s what children’s needs are all about. Kids also develop confidence when they know they matter just as much as anybody else.

JF: What are some behaviors that are normal for teens but that parents might misinterpret as pushback or misbehavior?

LG: Sometimes teens experiment with saying or doing things that clash with their socialization up to that point, such as the language they use or the clothes they wear. These are things that the parent can feel like, “Whoa, I’m uncomfortable with this…”.

Here are two meaningful ways to navigate these moments.

Ask your teen questions about what they’re into, such as the styles they like or what they admire about someone they idolize. Try showing interest, not intrusive interest, but just interest in what they like, or why they are experimenting with different things.

Keep in mind that when your teen snaps at you, is in a bad mood, or slams the door, their emotional centers are activated in a way that will probably never be repeated in their life because their brains prioritize emotional development first during this stage.

JF: Can you share more about why a teen’s development follows this trajectory?

LG: Yeah, I know it’s easy to ask, “Why in the world would nature do it that way?” It’s because that’s how important the emotional self and relationships are to our real success as independent adults.

As adults, we have to know ourselves inside and out and use our feelings to guide us. Teens are still trying to work this out. Learning how to handle these emotions takes a lot of practice. They’re finding out what it’s like to feel rage, or what it’s like to be in love, or to feel disappointed. And they’re feeling them in the most intense way they ever will, because the brain is taking on the job of developing them into a really deep, complete human being.

JF: What advice do you have for parents when their teen’s emotions push their own buttons?

LG: Keep in mind that when your teen responds in an adamant, emotional, defiant way, or calls you names, they’re not really in command of those emotions yet.

Instead of coming down hard with words that suggest they’re not a good person, try to respond with: “I’m really interested in how you feel about this. I want to hear your arguments, but when you call me a name, it makes it impossible for me to be available to you. It just doesn’t work. We don’t call each other names in this family. That won’t work when you’re an adult, either.”.

The interaction then becomes an education about how people respond to different kinds of approaches. Harshness that stops a teen cold shuts down their impulse to communicate their feelings to other people, which isn’t good for resilience or honest relationships.

JF: What are two things that parents do to foster emotional maturity that can actually backfire?

LG: One is the importance of achievement, of having a good resume. Of course, parents know how hard life is as an adult. We feel it’s our duty to convey these realizations to our kids. But when it becomes something that feels like everything else will fall into place if you do these things first or achieve X, we are not helping our kids with the emotional or interpersonal side of life. We’re creating a one-dimensional kind of person.

Sometimes parents also think that if they don’t give their child severe consequences or punishments, the child won’t learn and mature. When you try to convey information through punishment, you actually teach a child to defer to other people’s anger and control. Of course, we want them to be aware of consequences, but sometimes we can go too far. You can’t have a full, right life if you’re always anticipating that somebody might be mad at you.

Juli Fraga, Psy.D., is an AEDP-trained psychologist in San Francisco. She supports parents with kids of all ages. She is also the co-author of the new book, Parents Have Feelings, Too.

#127160. Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene

📅 19 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1458 w)

Why some people escape Alzheimer’s despite carrying a high-risk gene

📅 19 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1458 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s.
  • Sources indicate that now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance.
  • Recent findings suggest that the discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some people carry one of the strongest genetic risk factors for Alzheimer's disease yet never develop it, remaining mentally sharp well into their 80s. For years, scientists have wondered what protects these individuals despite their increased genetic vulnerability.

Sources indicate that now, researchers at Columbia University have uncovered a biological mechanism that could help explain this remarkable resistance. Their findings point to a rare genetic mutation that protects the brain's blood vessels from damage, potentially opening a fresh path toward Alzheimer's treatments.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery builds on research the team published two years ago involving APOE ε4, a gene variant strongly associated with Alzheimer's risk. The scientists found that some people carrying APOE ε4 also possess a rare protective mutation in the fibronectin (FN1) gene.

Fibronectin is a protein that helps support the structure of tissues. However, in people with APOE ε4, excessive amounts can accumulate around blood vessels in the brain, potentially compromising a critical protective system known as the blood-brain barrier. The rare FN1 mutation appears to limit this buildup and the damage associated with it.

That earlier discovery suggested an intriguing possibility: What if scientists could develop a treatment that recreates the protection provided by this rare mutation?

A upcoming study published in Nature Aging brings that possibility closer by identifying how excess fibronectin damages the brain's protective barrier and revealing potential ways to interrupt the process.

"This upcoming study takes us from a genetic clue to a disease mechanism," says Caghan Kizil, the study's corresponding author and professor of neurological sciences in the Department of Neurology and the Taub Institute for Research on Alzheimer's Disease and the Aging Brain at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons.

In a recent development, "We knew that changes in fibronectin could protect against Alzheimer's, but we didn't know why excess fibronectin was harmful in the first place. This study gives us that detailed mechanism -- and with it, ideas for how to reproduce that natural protection.".

How an Alzheimer's Risk Gene Weakens the Blood-Brain Barrier.

The blood-brain barrier serves as a protective boundary between the bloodstream and the brain. Made up of tightly connected cells surrounding the brain's blood vessels, it carefully regulates which substances can enter brain tissue while helping maintain conditions necessary for removing potentially harmful waste.

When this barrier becomes damaged or excessively permeable, substances that would normally be kept out can enter the brain more easily. Such disruptions may contribute to inflammation and other processes involved in neurological diseases, including Alzheimer's.

To investigate the role of fibronectin, the Columbia team combined several advanced research approaches. They examined human brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid surrounding the brain and spinal cord, using genetic and epigenetic analyses to explore changes in DNA and gene activity.

Sources indicate that their investigation also included single-cell sequencing, which reveals the activity of individual cells, and spatial imaging to examine where biological changes occur within tissues. Additional experiments involved human stem-cell models, three-dimensional cultures of blood vessels, and studies in zebrafish and mice.

Despite the variety of methods, the findings consistently pointed to the same mechanism: APOE ε4 promotes the production and accumulation of fibronectin around the brain's blood vessels.

In mice engineered to carry human APOE ε4, researchers measured nearly twice as much fibronectin in the brain as in mice carrying APOE ε3, another common version of the gene. The greater accumulation was accompanied by evidence that the blood-brain barrier had become leaky.

Scientists Discover How Fibronectin Causes Brain Damage.

One experiment provided especially important evidence that fibronectin does more than simply accumulate in damaged blood vessels.

The researchers increased human fibronectin specifically in astrocytes, specialized support cells that help maintain the blood-brain barrier and keep the brain functioning properly.

Increasing fibronectin in these cells was enough to disrupt the barrier, allowing it to become more permeable. Conversely, reducing fibronectin improved the barrier's ability to function normally.

These results provided experimental evidence that excess fibronectin can directly contribute to blood-brain barrier damage rather than merely appearing alongside it.

Recent findings suggest that "The animal experiments allowed us to move beyond association," notes co-first author Prabesh Bhattarai, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "When we increased fibronectin in astroglia, the barrier became permeable. When we reduced fibronectin, barrier function improved.".

The team then investigated the molecular events responsible for the damage.

They found that excessive fibronectin interferes with communication between cells by activating abnormal signals through integrins, proteins that help cells sense and respond to their surroundings, and an enzyme known as focal adhesion kinase.

Recent findings suggest that these abnormal signals disrupt a network of growth factors called VEGF, HBEGF, and IGF1. Although growth factors are often associated with cell development and repair, these particular signaling molecules also help astrocytes and blood vessel cells coordinate their activities to maintain a healthy blood-brain barrier.

When their communication becomes disrupted, the barrier can lose its integrity, potentially leaving brain tissue more vulnerable to damage.

"Single-cell analysis allowed us to examine this pathway in the different cells that maintain the brain's blood vessels," notes co-first author Elanur Yilmaz, an associate research scientist in the Kizil lab. "We observed the same biological pattern across experimental models and human Alzheimer's tissue, making the mechanism especially compelling.".

Evidence From Human Brains Strengthens the Alzheimer's Connection.

Importantly, the researchers found signs of similar biological disturbances in human samples, suggesting that the process identified in laboratory experiments may also contribute to Alzheimer's disease in people carrying APOE ε4.

Analyses of brain tissue and cerebrospinal fluid showed that elevated fibronectin levels were associated with inflammation in astrocytes.

Genetic and gene-regulation analyses also connected FN1 to blood vessel disease and changes involving VEGFA, a growth factor that plays an key role in maintaining healthy brain blood vessels.

Together, these findings provide multiple lines of evidence linking excess fibronectin to the vascular damage associated with APOE ε4.

"The convergence of these independent human datasets strengthens the case that fibronectin is part of the APOE ε4-related vascular disease process," states Badri Vardarajan, associate professor of neurological science in the Department of Neurology, Gertrude H. Sergievsky Center, and Taub Institute, who collaborated on this discovery of the FN1 mutation.

A Rare Genetic Defense Could Inspire Fresh Alzheimer's Treatments.

The potential implications are significant because APOE ε4 is the strongest common genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's disease. Approximately one in five people carries at least one copy of this gene variant.

Although carrying APOE ε4 does not guarantee that someone will develop Alzheimer's, it increases their likelihood of developing the disease. Understanding why certain carriers remain unaffected could reveal fresh opportunities for prevention and treatment.

The latest findings suggest several possible approaches.

One strategy would be to prevent harmful amounts of fibronectin from accumulating around the brain's blood vessels. Another would involve blocking the abnormal cellular signals triggered by excess fibronectin. A third possibility would be to restore the growth factor signaling that allows astrocytes and blood vessel cells to maintain the blood-brain barrier.

Researchers are already investigating these possibilities through laboratory experiments.

However, translating the discovery into a treatment will require considerable care. Fibronectin performs essential functions throughout the body, including supporting tissue structure and helping damaged tissues heal. Any future therapy would therefore need to target its harmful accumulation or effects without disrupting these beneficial activities.

By identifying the molecular mechanisms involved, scientists now have a more precise framework for designing such treatments. The findings may also help researchers determine when interventions would be most effective and how to measure whether they are successfully protecting the brain.

In a recent development, "By showing how fibronectin contributes to early vascular damage, this study gives us new therapeutic targets and potential ways to measure whether treatments are working," says Richard Mayeux, chair of the Department of Neurology and a collaborator on the project. "Clinically, it connects a major genetic risk factor for Alzheimer's to an early disease process that may be possible to modify.".

Sources indicate that although these potential therapies remain experimental, the discovery offers a promising upcoming direction in Alzheimer's research. Rather than focusing only on the damage that develops as the disease progresses, scientists may eventually be able to reproduce a natural genetic defense that helps protect vulnerable brains before significant damage occurs.

#127158. Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Neurosciencenews ↗ Open Full Page

Does Working Harder Make Learning Fun?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Neurosciencenews

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A fresh psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable.
  • Parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it.
  • Yet a new psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A fresh psychology study challenges the classic educational advice that simply putting in more effort makes learning enjoyable. Three experiments reveal that while cognitive effort improves comprehension, it does not spark curiosity or enjoyment, instead, preexisting interest motivates students to engage in the first place.

Parents and educators frequently repeat a familiar piece of advice when children groan over difficult homework: if you just try harder, you’ll start to enjoy it. Behind this common wisdom lies an intuitive assumption that sustained cognitive effort naturally blossoms into curiosity and intrinsic motivation.

Yet a new psychological investigation from Kyushu University suggests that this relationship works in the exact opposite direction.

Published in Acta Psychologica, the study demonstrates that forcing effort improves basic comprehension, but it does not make dry or unappealing material more interesting. Instead, genuine interest and liking come first—serving as the psychological spark that motivates learners to invest cognitive effort voluntarily.

Sources indicate that “I’m curious if a student is made to work harder, does that bring the same benefits as effort they choose to give,” asked Yimeng Jin, a doctoral student at Kyushu University’s Graduate School of Systems Life Sciences and first author of the study. “It matters because many learning environments rely on required effort, such as assignments, on the assumption that more effort is always better.”.

To disentangle voluntary motivation from mandatory mental exertion, Jin and senior author Professor Johan Lauwereyns at Kyushu University’s Faculty of Arts and Science conducted three behavioral experiments involving 110 university students.

According to recent reports, participants read pairs of seemingly unrelated sentences and decided whether they wanted to construct an explanation connecting them. By tracking participants’ initial choices, task completion, and time spent, the team isolated two distinct components of learning: willingness to engage and cognitive effort invested.

Across the three experimental phases, a clear cognitive pattern emerged:.

It has been revealed that “Interestingly, participants who were required to explain spent more time on the task than those who chose to do so,” Jin noted. “Perhaps they initially skipped it because the sentences were harder to understand, so they needed more time to make sense of them. It’s a bit like struggling through homework in a subject you don’t enjoy. Together, the experiments suggest that effort can help people make sense of information, while interest is more closely linked to their willingness to engage.”.

While the researchers caution that short laboratory reading tasks among university students differ from long-term classroom learning in younger children, the findings carry broad implications for how educators, parents, and communicators design learning environments. Rather than relying solely on mandatory drill work to manufacture enthusiasm, sparking authentic curiosity first may unlock deeper, faster comprehension.

“The findings have implications far outside education. The connection between engagement and effort is key whenever our understanding depends on reading texts,” concluded Lauwereyns.

Does working harder on a subject automatically make it more enjoyable?

It has been revealed that no. Researchers at Kyushu University found that while putting in cognitive effort helps students better understand difficult material, it does not increase their interest in or enjoyment of the subject.

What actually motivates students to put effort into learning?

Recent findings suggest that the experiments indicated that preexisting interest and liking come first. When students already find a topic intriguing, they are far more willing to engage voluntarily, and they comprehend the material more efficiently than when forced to work through topics they want to skip.

What happens when students are forced to work on material they don’t find interesting?

When participants were required to explain material they initially chose to skip, they spent significantly more time struggling with the task, gained less comprehension compared to voluntary effort, and indicated no increase in enjoyment.

Effort enhances understanding, while appreciation drives engagement in Cross-sentence semantic processing.

Industry observers note that comprehensive reading requires active semantic processing, going beyond explicitly stated information to construct connections and meaning. Building on discourse coherence theory, Reader-Response Theory and insights from Language Poetry, the present research investigates how active engagement and cognitive effort shape semantic processing.

We propose that evaluative dimensions central to aesthetic appreciation, namely understanding, interest, and liking, also play crucial roles in semantic processing.

To examine these processes, we developed a novel cross-sentence elaboration paradigm using unconnected, randomly paired sentences that create semantic gaps and encourage reader-driven meaning construction.

Industry observers note that in Experiment 1, participants could voluntarily invest effort by thinking aloud during elaboration. Results highlighted greater volitional engagement was associated with higher levels of understanding, interest, and appreciation.

Experiment 2 dissociated willingness to engage from actual effort, revealing that appreciation predicted participants’ willingness to invest further effort, whereas additional completed effort did not consistently increase appreciation.

Experiment 3 examined forced effort, showing that externally imposed effort enhanced semantic understanding but did not consistently increase appreciation, highlighting the distinct roles of volitional and imposed effort.

An integrated 2 × 2 analysis of Experiments 2 and 3 showed that active engagement and cognitive effort made distinct, interactive contributions to evaluation and processing time, with completed cognitive effort more reliably predicting accurate recognition memory and active engagement more closely tied to memory for the processing context.

Together, these findings clarify the interplay between engagement, effort, understanding, and appreciation, offering fresh insights into the cognitive dynamics of active meaning construction in semantic processing.

#127156. Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1444 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Your aging brain may be trading memory for something more valuable

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1444 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities.
  • Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging.
  • It has been revealed that the researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that growing older is often associated with memory loss and declining mental abilities. However, scientists are questioning whether these changes tell the whole story. Rather than simply becoming less capable, the brain may be adapting to a latest stage of life in which accumulated knowledge, wisdom, and understanding become more important than remembering every detail.

Sources indicate that researchers at the University of Arizona have proposed a different way of understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on findings from molecular biology and brain imaging, they suggest that the changes occurring in older brains may reflect a natural stage of human development rather than deterioration alone. Their work, published in Perspectives on Psychological Science, offers a upcoming perspective on why thinking and memory change with age.

It has been revealed that the researchers call their proposed explanation the adaptive aging hypothesis. It suggests that the brain gradually adjusts its priorities to make better use of a lifetime of accumulated experience. This could help explain why older adults often have valuable strengths in teaching, mentoring, storytelling, and passing knowledge to younger generations.

Sources indicate that "If we look at normative aging as a story of just decline, we are really missing the boat," said study coauthor Fabian-Xosé Fernandez, an associate professor of cognition and neural systems at the University of Arizona. "The older brain is optimized for different things than the younger brain, predominantly the sharing of stored expertise and social relationships.".

How the Brain Shifts From Memory to Meaning.

Two brain regions play important roles in how people remember and interpret their experiences. The hippocampus helps preserve specific information about events, including their details and circumstances. The frontal cortex, meanwhile, is more involved in extracting broader meaning, recognizing patterns, and understanding the central message of an experience, sometimes called its "gist.".

According to the researchers, the balance between these systems changes during healthy aging. As people grow older, the brain tends to place less emphasis on activity in the hippocampus and rely more on the frontal cortex. This shift may allow the brain to focus more on interpreting information through existing knowledge rather than recording every newly introduced experience in precise detail.

In a recent development, "The fact that you see this across people and animal models suggests there is an evolutionary driving force," Fernandez said. "One could argue you are developing your entire life, and development occurs in lockstep with the needs of your brain. When you're younger, the hippocampus turns on because you don't have a knowledge base or know how the world works. A kid absorbs information like a sponge because they are building an archive of information. In early life, the balance is tilted toward recollecting declarative memories with precision, detail, and context.".

According to recent reports, young brains need to gather enormous amounts of new information because they are still building a foundation for understanding the world. By later adulthood, however, people have already developed extensive stores of memories, concepts, and experiences. Connecting new information to what they already know may become more useful than retaining every individual detail.

The researchers suggest that this changing balance reflects a shift in how the brain processes experience. Instead of concentrating primarily on collecting detailed memories, it increasingly emphasizes understanding relationships, identifying underlying meaning, and applying previously acquired knowledge.

Why Evolution May Favor Wisdom in Older Adults.

In a recent development, evidence of similar changes in animal models raises the possibility that this transition has an evolutionary explanation. Fernandez suggests that the aging brain may be adapting to help individuals preserve and share the knowledge they have acquired throughout their lives.

Industry observers note that from this perspective, the ability to draw on decades of experience could be especially valuable for making judgments, guiding others, and transferring vital information between generations. Older adults may therefore play a distinct role in supporting younger people through mentorship, teaching, and storytelling.

Industry observers note that "Given those goals, it makes sense that you aren't interested in nitty-gritty details," Fernandez mentioned. "You are interested in safeguarding the vast knowledge you already have. Evolution may be saying that if you make it long enough, there's a need to transmit this information, so we put into motion biological changes that enforce and protect your semantic and autobiographical memories.".

Under this hypothesis, changes in memory and thinking are not necessarily signs that the brain is functioning less effectively. They may instead reflect a different set of priorities, with greater emphasis on preserving meaningful knowledge and using it to understand new situations.

Why Healthy Brain Aging Is Different From Alzheimer's.

The adaptive aging hypothesis could also provide scientists with another way to examine the differences between normal cognitive aging and Alzheimer's disease.

It has been revealed that although both involve changes in memory, Fernandez emphasizes that Alzheimer's should not be understood as ordinary aging taken to an extreme. The biological processes involved are fundamentally different.

According to recent reports, "When I was in grad school, people thought about Alzheimer's as a more intense version of cognitive aging, but that is just not the case," Fernandez mentioned. "They are completely different.".

During typical aging, the brain's gradual shift away from relying heavily on the hippocampus and toward greater involvement of the frontal cortex generally unfolds between the fifth and seventh decades of life. In Alzheimer's disease, however, abnormal processes involving proteins such as amyloid and tau may interfere with this transition.

Recent findings suggest that one key distinction involves activity in the hippocampus. While healthy aging is generally associated with reduced emphasis on this region, Alzheimer's can involve unusually high levels of hippocampal activity. Rather than supporting the normal progression of cognitive development, disease-related changes may disrupt the brain networks responsible for memory and understanding.

Industry observers note that "In normative aging, hippocampal activation is deemphasized, which is probably what should be happening in a 70-year-old. But in many cases of Alzheimer's, it turns out the hippocampus is hyperactive," he said. "This beautiful developmental transition is completely disrupted in Alzheimer's disease by pathological processes that mess with episodic memory and interfere with circuits that allow you to think about your own life, lexicon, and vocabulary.".

In a recent development, these disruptions can affect the ability to recall personal experiences and access stored knowledge, including words and their meanings. Understanding how these changes differ from the adaptations associated with healthy aging may help researchers develop a clearer picture of normal brain development and neurodegenerative disease.

Embracing the Hidden Strengths of the Aging Brain.

Industry observers note that the researchers argue that society may need to reconsider what successful brain aging looks like. Encouraging older adults to process information exactly as younger people do may not always be the most productive approach.

Fernandez suggests that placing excessive emphasis on remembering precise details could work against the brain's changing priorities. "For many individuals, the weight of how you process information should probably not be so hippocampal-centric by the sixth or seventh decade.".

Instead of judging older adults primarily by abilities that tend to weaken with age, the researchers encourage greater recognition of the capabilities that may become especially valuable later in life.

Recent findings suggest that creating more opportunities for social interaction could be one way to support these strengths. Relationships between older and younger generations may be particularly beneficial because they provide opportunities to exchange experiences, share expertise, and preserve knowledge that might otherwise be lost.

"People see older individuals and look at them as not being on par with younger individuals across a lot of metrics," Fernandez states. "The way I look at it is that you've got someone with a brain that has been active for several decades and has seen a lot. There is tremendous value there, and we don't do a good job of unlocking it.".

The central message of the adaptive aging hypothesis is that growing older may involve more than a gradual reduction in cognitive abilities. Although some mental skills become less reliable with age, the brain may also be adapting to make better use of the knowledge and experience accumulated over a lifetime. Recognizing those strengths could change how society understands aging and the contributions older adults can make.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers dramatically accelerated electron tomography to map large volumes of brain tissue at 15-nanometer 3D resolution.
  • Recent findings suggest that to understand how billions of neurons orchestrate thoughts, memories, and movement, neuroscientists construct connectomes, detailed wiring diagrams mapping how brain cells connect and communicate.
  • As a result, even the most ambitious brain wiring maps have routinely missed ultra-fine cellular architectures, including electrical synapses (also called gap junctions), microscopic channels that enable direct, near-instantaneous electrical communication between adjacent neurons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers dramatically accelerated electron tomography to map large volumes of brain tissue at 15-nanometer 3D resolution. The breakthrough captures fine neural structures missed by conventional connectomes, including rapid-fire electrical synapses and uncharacterized protrusions where neurons appear to “nibble” neighboring glial cells.

Recent findings suggest that to understand how billions of neurons orchestrate thoughts, memories, and movement, neuroscientists construct connectomes, detailed wiring diagrams mapping how brain cells connect and communicate. While macro-scale MRI scans chart major white-matter highways and standard electron microscopy traces individual chemical synapses, scaling up to large tissue volumes has historically forced a difficult compromise: sacrificing nanoscale structural detail for imaging speed.

As a result, even the most ambitious brain wiring maps have routinely missed ultra-fine cellular architectures, including electrical synapses (also called gap junctions), microscopic channels that enable direct, near-instantaneous electrical communication between adjacent neurons.

Now, in a study published November 19 in Nature Methods, researchers at Harvard Medical School (HMS) and the University of California San Diego have overcome that bottleneck by supercharging electron tomography—a 3D imaging technique that reconstructs nanoscale architecture by tilting tissue samples and capturing views from multiple angles.

Led by co-senior authors Dr. Wei-Chung Allen Lee (associate professor of neurobiology at HMS and associate professor of neurology at Boston Children’s Hospital) and Dr. Mark Ellisman (UC San Diego), alongside co-first authors Dr. Aaron T. Kuan and Dr. Sébastien Phan, the team demonstrated that large blocks of brain tissue can be mapped in exquisite 3D nanoscale detail without prohibitive imaging times.

Conventional electron tomography is painstakingly slow because it typically requires capturing hundreds of tilted images across razor-thin tissue slices. By refining image acquisition and computational reconstruction, Lee, Ellisman, and colleagues discovered they could cut the required number of images by roughly 50-fold while imaging tissue sections 20 times thicker than standard electron microscopy protocols, preserving an extraordinary 3D resolution of 15 nanometers or finer.

Recent findings suggest that “We can now see brain structures that we haven’t been able to see before in connectomics data,” explained Lee. “We hope this work will help us understand how nervous systems are built; what changes with age; and what goes awry in neurodevelopmental, cognitive, and neurodegenerative disorders.”.

When the researchers applied their high-speed tomography pipeline to tissue from the mouse cerebellum, the 3D reconstructions revealed both long-sought neural connections and surprising cellular behaviors:.

“We’re seeing uncharacterized structures, suggesting that neurons are ‘nibbling’ their neighboring cells,” Lee mentioned.

In addition, the researchers traced delicate nerve fibers continuously through the thick 3D tissue block right down to their exact synaptic contact points with target neurons.

While scaling this accelerated tomography workflow to map an entire mammalian brain will require automated tissue-handling robotics, the breakthrough bridges a critical resolution gap in modern connectomics—equipping neuroscientists to examine how fine electrical and glial-neuronal connections form in early life and break down in brain disease.

Why do traditional brain wiring maps (connectomes) miss certain structures?

Mapping large volumes of brain tissue at high speed usually forces scientists to sacrifice ultra-fine resolution. As a result, critical microscopic features, such as tiny electrical synapses (gap junctions) that connect neurons directly, often blur out or go undetected in large-scale datasets.

How did researchers speed up nanoscale 3D brain imaging?

The team optimized electron tomography so that it requires about 50 times fewer multi-angle images on tissue slices 20 times thicker than usual, while still maintaining a 3D resolution of 15 nanometers or finer.

What surprising newly introduced structures did they see in the brain tissue?

Alongside hard-to-see electrical synapses in the mouse cerebellum, the researchers discovered tiny protrusions between neurons and neighboring support cells (glia), suggesting that neurons physically “nibble” or take up material from adjacent cells.

Funding: This work was supported by the National Institutes of Health (grants RF1MH129261, U01NS142013, and K99EB032217), with startup support to Kuan from the Yale School of Medicine Department of Neuroscience and Wu Tsai Institute.

Harvard University filed a patent application regarding GridTape (WO2017184621A1) on behalf of inventors, including Lee, and negotiated licensing agreements with interested partners. All other authors have no competing interests.

Scalable electron tomography for connectomics.

We demonstrate limited-tilt, serial-section electron tomography (ET), which can non-destructively map brain circuits over large 3D volumes and provide high-resolution, supramolecular details within subvolumes of interest.

Here we show accelerated ET imaging of semi-thick sections ( >500 nm) from the mouse cerebellar cortex, with 3D resolution <15 nm and machine learning-based image augmentation, providing the capacity to resolve key features of neuronal circuits including chemical synapses, endocytic structures and gap junctions.

Furthermore, we systematically assess how imaging parameters affect image quality and speed to enable connectomic-scale projects.

The gift tax is one of the most misunderstood parts of the tax code. People hear "gift tax" and assume they'll owe the IRS money for giving a birthday check to their grandchild. That's almost never how it works. The federal gift tax exists to prevent people from giving away their entire estate during their lifetime to dodge estate taxes at death. For the vast majority of Americans, it will never cost them a dime.

Here's what actually matters: in 2026, you can give up to $18,000 to any individual without reporting it to the IRS at all. Give that amount to 10 different people and you've transferred $180,000 completely under the radar. Go above the annual limit and you still won't owe tax — you'll just file a form that tracks the excess against your $13.61 million lifetime exemption.

Recent findings suggest that the gift tax is really a planning tool, not a penalty. Understanding how it works can help you transfer wealth to family members, fund education, reduce your taxable estate, and accelerate your heirs' path to financial independence — all without triggering any actual tax.

It has been revealed that the annual gift tax exclusion is the amount you can give to any single recipient each year without needing to file a gift tax return or use any of your lifetime exemption. For 2026, that amount is $18,000 per recipient.

The annual exclusion has roughly doubled since 2002, when it was just $11,000. Inflation adjustments are made in $1,000 increments, so the number stays flat for a year or two, then bumps up.

This is the single most notable gift tax fact: the person making the gift is responsible for any gift tax — never the recipient. If your grandmother gives you $50,000, she files the gift tax return and uses her lifetime exemption. You don't report it as income, you don't owe tax on it, and you don't need to do anything. When you give more than the annual exclusion to any single person, the excess counts against your lifetime gift and estate tax exemption — presently $13.61 million per person ($27.22 million for married couples). You won't actually owe gift tax until you've exceeded this lifetime amount.

Should We Look to Hunter-Gatherer Societies as Models of Equality?

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1060 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food.
  • It has been revealed that news spreads like wildfire across the camp.
  • Industry observers note that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the shores of Lake Eyasi in Northern Tanzania, a small number of people still hunt and gather their food. Today a Hadza hunter has taken down an animal—a kudu. He can’t carry it by himself, so he cuts his poisoned arrow from its flank, covers the carcass in dry grass to hide it from hyenas, and heads home to enlist help.

It has been revealed that news spreads like wildfire across the camp. Everybody rushes to the kill. They divide up the carcass, carry it back, then divvy it up some more. Every family gets some, and after the meat is cooked, there’s more sharing still. On a good day like today, the hunter and his family retain half, but sometimes they keep much less. People may even walk from other camps, and almost everyone, from miles around, is entitled to a share.

Industry observers note that the post-hunt scene above is idyllic. It paints a quintessential picture of egalitarianism and equality. But our experience as anthropologists working with the Hadza people of Tanzania and with the Tsimane people of Bolivia’s Amazon rainforest is that inequalities are part of even the most equal of societies. Furthermore, the equalities that do exist often emerge from selfish motives.

Insights like ours are revising researchers’ understanding of both the past and how people operate today, as inequality grows globally. Hunter-gatherers are often at the center of heated academic battles about what it means to be human, including debates over gender, war, and peace and whether humans are, by nature, egalitarian or hierarchical.

Sometimes these debates oversimplify. So we pulled together hundreds of different sources covering more than a century of ethnography to find out just how egalitarian hunter-gatherer and other subsistence societies really are.

Anthropologists have called hunter-gatherers such as the Hadza “egalitarian societies,” with equalities of power, wealth, and social status. And it’s true that the traditional subsistence communities we work with successfully limit many inequalities.

Most families have similar, modest possessions and store little material wealth. When leaders do emerge, they are highly constrained in how they can direct other people. People often make decisions via consensus, and, if they cannot reach agreement, families will move away.

While the same anthropologists also emphasize that some hunter-gatherers are very unequal and that equality takes deliberate effort, the prevailing impression is that equality characterizes hunter-gatherers, past and present.

A quick trip to your local bookshop will reveal grand claims, including that past hunter-gatherer societies had no permanent leadership and no hierarchy, inequality only spread with the development of agriculture, and humans are noble by nature.

Some scientists are pushing back against these utopian portrayals. The popular bestseller, The Dawn of Everything, calls egalitarianism a “Garden of Eden narrative” that lacks substance. Other scholars have called egalitarian societies a scientific origin myth.

So where does the truth lie? Probably somewhere in between.

In our recent wide-ranging review of the evidence from the early 20th century onward, we found that no society lacked inequality.

Like the Hadza, the Ju/’Hoansi of the Kalahari desert in southern Africa had little property and widespread food-sharing, yet certain families controlled valuable hunting territory surrounding waterholes. The Bayaka of the central African rainforest had little material inequality, yet they bought, sold, and hoarded ritual knowledge. The Philippine Agta controlled and arranged their children’s marriages, hugely discriminating against orphans.

Gender inequalities were commonplace. The Tanzanian Hadza keep certain cuts of meat exclusively for older men, and give more respect to better hunters. Across societies, women have universally done more direct parenting, and men have participated more frequently in community-level decision making.

In a recent development, no society lacks informal leadership. Age was another source of inequality. In many Australian societies, older men controlled ritual secrets and had power over the marriage choices of younger relatives.

Sources indicate that our study also found that although hunter-gatherers are frequently generous, the processes limiting inequality often do not require any generosity. Instead, equality often results from people’s self-interested motives to acquire resources, status, and autonomy.

According to recent reports, A great example of this is food-sharing. Although each Hadza family gets a cut of kudu meat, it often happens not because the hunter’s family prioritizes total equality, but because other families request it vociferously. It can involve more taking than giving, often through strongly stated demands or complaints.

Another example is ridicule and mockery of stingy or braggadocious individuals, which keeps greed and bravado in check. Paradoxically, status-seeking can also promote equality, when cooperating to gain status diffuses status throughout the community.

Many of these inequality-reducing processes are familiar to people everywhere.

In a recent development, ridicule and mockery are ubiquitous in industrialized societies, from political cartoons to social media. Lampooning authority is even common in autocratic societies where governments spend large sums of money suppressing speech. Demands and complaints form the basis of strikes and collective bargaining. And key to social mobility is cooperation among people of different social strata.

Sources indicate that like many great debates, the truth is complex: Our ancient hunter-gatherer ancestors didn’t reach the giddy heights of inequality seen in other societies over the last 6,000 years, but putting hunter-gatherers on a pedestal as paragons of equality is a mistake. Sweeping statements about equality in the past blind us to the tools that probably allowed ancient hunter-gatherers to combat inequality, just as they and people in all societies do today.

Industry observers note that egalitarianism, then, is best seen not as perfect equality but as a set of tools that people use to secure their own autonomy and access to resources. Equality along one dimension or another might be the outcome, but it doesn’t rely on people being amazingly noble or completely lacking in greed or status-seeking. If you consider egalitarianism as equality-creating processes, you can see that it is a widespread reality among hunter-gatherer societies, and beyond.

Industry observers note that an international consortium has created personalized biophysical “digital brain twins” for 6,986 individuals across 16 countries to uncover how aging, neurodegenerative diseases, and environmental conditions shape neural dynamics. The computational models simulate excitation-inhibition balance across 90 connected brain regions, revealing distinct mechanistic signatures for Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal degeneration, and environmental exposures ranging from air pollution to democratic governance.

Standard magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) provides an invaluable window into the living human brain, yet it records only indirect proxies of neural activity, typically relying on group averages that obscure individual variation and say little about the underlying cellular mechanisms driving those signals.

Now, an international research team led by corresponding author Dr. Agustín Ibáñez (Scientific Director of BrainLat at Universidad Adolfo Ibáñez, strategic director of core scientific assets at the BarcelonaBeta Brain Research Center, and faculty at the Global Brain Health Institute at Trinity College Dublin) and first author Dr. Rubén Herzog (BrainLat and Distinguished Professor at the University of the Balearic Islands) has transformed static brain scans into dynamic, personalized virtual laboratories.

Published today in Nature Biomedical Engineering, the study introduces biophysical “digital brain twins” constructed from resting-state functional MRI (fMRI) scans of 6,986 individuals spanning ages 18 to 100 across 16 countries.

Rather than treating brain scans as passive statistical snapshots, biophysical brain twins apply mathematical equations grounded in neurobiology to simulate how populations of excitatory and inhibitory neurons interact across 90 connected brain regions.

In a recent development, for each participant, the investigators tuned their computational model until its simulated fMRI output closely matched the individual’s actual resting-state brain recordings. Independent validation demonstrated that model-derived regional excitability closely correlated with structural grey matter volume, confirming that the virtual simulations capture real biological architecture.

Industry observers note that “Every brain ages in a different context. Our biophysical twins help us study how the variations in our biology and the social and environmental conditions of our lives relate to brain function,” explained Ibáñez. “The importance of biophysical brain twins is that they connect what brain scans record with the underlying processes that could produce those signals. Each twin acts as a personalised virtual laboratory: researchers can adjust how its neural populations interact and examine how those changes affect the whole brain. This opens a route from observing differences to testing possible explanations, mechanisms, potential treatments and interventions.”.

“MRI records indirect measures of neural activity. Biophysical twins let us simulate the neural processes that might generate those signals and explore why they differ from person to person,” added Herzog.

Applying these nearly 7,000 personalized models across diverse clinical cohorts exposed clear mechanistic boundaries between normal aging and dementia:.

To overcome the historical divide between neuroimaging and real-world lived context, the team linked individual brain models with macro-level environmental indicators across 10 domains alongside personal socioeconomic histories.

Robust associations emerged in seven of the ten environmental domains, most prominently in indicators measuring democratic conditions (free choices, civic participation, political representation, and rule of law), soil and water quality, and air pollution. Complementary analyses of individual life circumstances further linked brain dynamics to healthcare access, childhood experiences, and financial stability. These relationships persisted even after controlling for age, sex, clinical diagnosis, country, and MRI scanner hardware.

Recent findings suggest that by releasing their open-source code and model parameters, the authors have established a global testbed for in silico experimentation. Future studies can overlay neurotransmitter receptor maps onto these digital twins—simulating how targeted modulation of glutamate (excitatory) or GABA (inhibitory) signaling, or public health improvements in air quality and healthcare access, might shift an aging brain back toward healthy functional patterns.

What is a biophysical “digital brain twin”?

Industry observers note that A digital brain twin is a personalized computer simulation built from an individual’s fMRI scan using biological equations. By modeling how 90 connected brain regions interact, it allows researchers to estimate underlying cellular processes, such as the balance between signals that excite or inhibit neurons—and test virtual treatments safely on a computer.

How do brain dynamics differ between normal aging and dementia?

Recent findings suggest that in the study of nearly 7,000 people, normal aging primarily changed how regularly or unpredictably brain activity fluctuated over time. In contrast, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal degeneration disrupted overall activity levels, variability, and the balance between excitatory and inhibitory brain signals all at once.

Can environmental and social conditions really affect how the brain functions?

Yes. Even after accounting for age, sex, diagnosis, and scanner differences, researchers found that environmental factors, especially democratic conditions, soil and water quality, air pollution, healthcare access, and financial circumstances, were measurably linked to underlying simulated brain dynamics.

Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype–expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.

Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological–environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics.

Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia.

Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure–function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes.

Sources indicate that associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research.

These findings ground phenotypic–exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

#127151. Breaking: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit

Breaking: Millions take fish oil for brain health. A two-year study found no benefit

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1362 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Millions of Americans take fish oil supplements in hopes of protecting their memory and keeping their brains healthy as they age.
  • But a new study suggests that getting more omega-3s into the brain through supplements may not provide the protection many people expect.
  • Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC found that even when high doses of omega-3s successfully reached the brain, they did not produce measurable improvements in memory, thinking abilities, or protection against brain shrinkage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Millions of Americans take fish oil supplements in hopes of protecting their memory and keeping their brains healthy as they age. These products have become a major business, with Americans spending more than $1 billion each year on supplements containing omega-3 fatty acids. These essential nutrients help build and maintain the connections between brain cells that support memory, learning, and other cognitive functions.

But a new study suggests that getting more omega-3s into the brain through supplements may not provide the protection many people expect.

Researchers at Keck Medicine of USC found that even when high doses of omega-3s successfully reached the brain, they did not produce measurable improvements in memory, thinking abilities, or protection against brain shrinkage.

The findings, published in eBioMedicine, come from a two-year clinical trial involving older adults considered to be at increased risk of developing Alzheimer's disease. Despite taking omega-3 supplements daily, participants showed no significant cognitive advantage over those who received a placebo.

Sources indicate that "We all wish there was a silver bullet for preventing Alzheimer's, but our findings showed that fish oil supplements do not appear to protect brain health," said Hussein Naji Yassine, MD, director of the USC Center for Personalized Brain Health and lead investigator of the study. "While omega-3s play an crucial role in forming brain cell connections needed for cognition, our results do not support fish oil supplements as a preventive measure against Alzheimer's.".

A Two-Year Study Tests Fish Oil's Brain Benefits.

In a recent development, to investigate whether omega-3 supplements could protect the aging brain, researchers enrolled 365 adults between the ages of 55 and 80. All participants rarely ate fish, a major dietary source of omega-3 fatty acids, and were considered at elevated risk for Alzheimer's disease.

Nearly half (47%) carried APOE4, a gene variant associated with a substantially higher risk of developing Alzheimer's later in life. Although having this variant does not mean someone will necessarily develop the disease, it is the strongest known genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's.

It has been revealed that participants were randomly assigned to receive either a daily fish oil supplement or a placebo, an inactive treatment used for comparison. The supplements provided 2,000 mg of docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), an omega-3 fatty acid that is especially important for the brain.

DHA is a major component of brain cell membranes, helping maintain the structure and function of neurons. It also supports communication between nerve cells, making it an important nutrient for normal brain activity.

The study was double-blind, meaning neither participants nor researchers knew who was receiving the active supplement during the trial. This approach helps reduce bias and makes it easier to determine whether any observed benefits are actually caused by the treatment.

Omega-3 Levels Rose, but Memory Did Not Improve.

Before evaluating whether the supplements improved brain health, researchers needed to answer a fundamental question: Were the omega-3 fatty acids actually reaching the brain?

To find out, they measured DHA concentrations in cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that surrounds and cushions the brain and spinal cord. Examining this fluid can provide information about substances entering and circulating within the central nervous system.

After six months, DHA levels in the cerebrospinal fluid had increased by an average of 17% among participants taking the supplements. This provided evidence that the omega-3 fatty acids were reaching their intended destination.

However, getting DHA into the central nervous system was only part of the goal. The more key question was whether those higher levels would translate into better brain health.

Researchers assessed participants' memory and other cognitive abilities at the beginning of the trial and again after two years. Despite the increase in DHA, those taking fish oil performed no better on the cognitive tests than participants receiving the placebo.

Brain imaging revealed similarly disappointing results.

It has been revealed that the supplements did not prevent shrinkage of the hippocampus, a region deep within the brain that plays a central role in forming and organizing memories. The hippocampus is particularly vulnerable to changes associated with aging and Alzheimer's disease, making its size an important indicator researchers use when studying brain health.

Taken together, the results suggest that simply increasing DHA availability in the brain is not enough to produce measurable cognitive benefits in this group of older adults.

Why Fish Oil Supplements May Work Differently Than Food.

The unexpected findings have raised a latest question for researchers: If omega-3s can reach the brain, why don't higher levels necessarily improve its function?

Yassine and his colleagues are now investigating how the brain absorbs, processes, and uses these nutrients. Their earlier research suggests that omega-3s may be more beneficial when consumed as part of a broader dietary pattern rather than taken in isolation as a supplement.

One possibility involves the Mediterranean-style diet, which emphasizes foods such as fish, vegetables, fruits, whole grains, legumes, nuts, and olive oil. This eating pattern naturally supplies omega-3 fatty acids alongside other nutrients and has been associated with a lower risk of Alzheimer's disease.

The researchers suspect that the combination of nutrients in a balanced diet, along with an individual's overall health, may influence how effectively omega-3s support the brain.

According to recent reports, "We're focused on better understanding how the brain processes omega-3s and whether factors, such as poor health, dietary pattern, genetic risk and age, may change the brain's ability to effectively absorb and use omega-3s," said Yassine. "We are working to develop medications that may help the brain better utilize these nutrients to preserve cognitive function.".

Understanding these differences could eventually help scientists identify why certain people might respond better to omega-3s than others and whether latest treatments could improve the brain's ability to benefit from these essential fats.

Sources indicate that importantly, the findings do not mean omega-3 fatty acids are unnecessary or that eating fish offers no health benefits. Instead, they indicate that taking high-dose DHA supplements alone did not provide measurable protection against cognitive decline or hippocampal shrinkage in the population studied.

Healthy Habits Remain Key to Alzheimer's Prevention.

Although the trial focused specifically on fish oil supplements, the researchers emphasize that protecting brain health requires a much broader approach.

Rather than relying on a single supplement, they recommend maintaining healthy habits throughout life, including regular physical activity, sufficient high-quality sleep, and a nutritious, balanced diet.

Industry observers note that these behaviors support overall health and may help reduce factors associated with cognitive decline. Physical exercise, for example, promotes cardiovascular health and blood flow, while sleep plays an crucial role in memory formation and normal brain maintenance.

"Staying healthy throughout life remains the most powerful tool we have for reducing Alzheimer's risk, including regular exercise, quality sleep and a balanced diet," said Yassine. "Living a healthy lifestyle is the brain's equivalent of getting regular car maintenance and high-quality oil changes. The brain is more likely to lose greater function if health complications in other parts of the body go unaddressed, in the same way that car engines stop working if regular maintenance is skipped.".

While these lifestyle factors were not directly tested in the trial, the researchers believe they offer a more promising foundation for long-term brain health than depending on fish oil supplements alone.

Sources indicate that the results also highlight an notable distinction: A nutrient can be essential for healthy brain function without providing additional protection when consumed in large doses as a supplement. Understanding why that happens may open new avenues for research into Alzheimer's prevention and the nutritional needs of the aging brain.

The research was supported by the National Institutes of Health, grant numbers RF1AG076124, R01AG055770, R01AG067063, R01AG054434, R21AG056518, P30AG066530 and R01AG054434 and the Alzheimer's Drug Discovery Foundation, grant number GC-201711-2014197.
